          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. There are 96 interlocutory applications today before us.
2. Ms. Anubha Agrawal, the learned counsel appearing for the
Board has taken pains to prepare a brief response to each and every
I.A. served on her as on 14.10.2026.
3. The note which she has prepared, includes the I.A. number, the
name of the AOR, the name of the customer/applicant, the prayer(s)
in the I.A. and response of the Management.
4. It will be difficult for us to take up each and every I.A.
today and hear the learned counsel appearing for the parties.
Instead, we request the learned counsel appearing for the Board to
furnish one copy each of this brief response to all the Advocates-
on-Record  who  are  appearing  in  the  individual  interlocutory
applications.
5. The learned counsel appearing for the Board would submit that
soft copies have already been forwarded on e-mail to all the AORs.
6. We request the learned counsel appearing in each of these
interlocutory applications to look into the response and if need
be, we shall hear it accordingly.
7. We are informed by some of the learned counsel appearing in
the matter that many open plots of the company have been encroached
upon. This is something very serious. And if the encroachment
continues, it will be difficult one fine day to remove the
encroachment all of a sudden.
8. In  such  circumstances,  we  request  the  learned  counsel
appearing for the Board to give a list of all those properties over
26

--- Page 44 ---
which there is illegal encroachment to the CEO NOIDA and one copy
to the Police Commissioner, Gautam Buddh Nagar.
9. We direct the Police Commissioner, Gautam Buddh Nagar, CEO
NOIDA and the District Magistrate, Gautam Buddh Nagar to ensure
that each and every encroachment on these plots are removed at the
earliest. An appropriate report in this regard be filed before us
by the next date of hearing.
10. The encroachment should not hamper the further progress,
insofar as the construction work which is to commence is concerned.
We are talking about the encroachments in Sectors 96, 97 and 98,
respectively, Noida under the name of Maya Nagar. The Police
Administration to act immediately.
11. List  the  interlocutory  application  Nos.  261064/2025,
180886/2025, 251540/2025, 330110/2025, 286435/2024, 305402/2026,
305405/2026  and  9000-9002/2025  in  C.A.  No.10856/2016  and

                             O R D E R
Heard Ms. Mukta Gupta, learned Senior Counsel/Head of
the Committee appointed by this Court along with Mr. S.D.
Sanjay, Coordinator and Convener, Dr. P.M. Nair, Committee
Member,  Ms.  Aparna  Bhat,  learned  Senior  Counsel  and
Committee Member, Ms. Archana Pathak Dave, learned A.S.G.
and other learned counsel for the parties.
2. In her submissions, Ms. Mukta Gupta, learned Senior
Counsel, the most serious issue which she has flagged
relates to substantive number of Police Stations all over
the country not being connected by a common internet
platform and in some cases the Police Stations not even
having a system on which they can upload the details of
the cases pending in that Police Station. In today’s
world, where every office is supposed to have a digitized
set up/computer facility for digitizing the data related
to the working of that office, Police Stations not having
such facility is absolutely unacceptable.
3. For the present, we refrain from taking a strict view
and passing severe orders against the concerned States. We
give them one last opportunity to ensure that all Police
Stations are digitally connected, latest within one month
from  today.  As  a  consequence,  all  First  Information
Reports would be also mandatorily uploaded on the said
7

--- Page 72 ---
SLP (CRL.) NO.11263/2025
computer, which in turn, through the internet would also
be uploaded on the concerned portal, both at the State
level, if any, and the national portal, i.e., CCTNS. We
clarify here that in cases where privacy issues may be
involved or there may be some data which may be sensitive
for national security, to that extent such data may be
redacted/not specified while uploading on the portals,
national  or  State,  though  to  be  maintained  in  the
concerned Police Station.
4. We clarify that within one month all Police Stations
to be equipped with basic hardware material relating to
digitization/computerization  with  the  facility  of
internet, either through a dedicated line or by way of a
dongle etc. Similarly, the Child Welfare Committees (CWCs)
be also digitized/computerized within the same period of
one month from today.
5. Such compliance shall be monitored and ensured by the
respective  Chief  Secretary/Home  Secretary  as  also  the
Director  Generals  of  Police  of  the  States/Union
Territories (UTs) and also Secretary, Women and Child
Welfare Department or any other administrative department
of the CWC. The Chief Secretary and the Finance Secretary
of the concerned State/UT shall ensure that sufficient
funds are provided for such digitization/computerization.
We indicate here that the equipments chosen shall not be
8

--- Page 73 ---
SLP (CRL.) NO.11263/2025
in a manner where just because under the garb of this
order, obsolete equipments at higher rates are taken and
there  shall  be  strict  monitoring  of  the  procurement
process so that the up-to-date technology of the day is
bought and the prices are fixed or paid in accordance with
law, for which the Director General/In-charge of Vigilance
Department of the concerned State/UTs shall be a member of
the Procurement Committee. The specifications for the same
would  be  universal  and  as  specified  by  the  NIC.  We
indicate that the Director of the NIC shall personally
form a team to provide the specifications and if it comes
to the notice of the Court that there has been any
deviation from the two principles of up-to-date technology
and the prices which can be negotiated to the benefit of
the  State  Exchequer  has  not  been  kept  in  mind,  the
Director,  NIC  and  the  Procurement  Committee  shall  be
personally  liable  to  answer  this  Court.  Under  no
circumstances the equipments shall be brought from the GeM
Portal of the Union.
6. Ms. Mukta Gupta, learned Senior Counsel has indicated
to the Court that in Paragraph 4(ii) of the order dated
22.05.2026, there is a direction to the Head of the Police
force of the concerned district to forward a copy of the
FIR to the jurisdictional Court in cases where the missing
person is restored to his/her family within 24 hours and
9

--- Page 74 ---
SLP (CRL.) NO.11263/2025
the matter to stand closed at that level itself. She has
indicated that there may be instances where recovery may
have been been made within 24 hours, but the reason for
the person to go missing may be a criminal offence or a
crime. We appreciate the assistance of Ms. Mukta Gupta in
indicating  that  the  said  order  needs  appropriate
clarification. Accordingly, the said direction would be
with a caveat that if the missing person is restored to
his/her family member within 24 hours, the statement of
the person shall be recorded and only if it indicates that
the  so  called  missing  of  the  person  was  inadvertent
without any criminal role attributed to any other person,
in such case only, the said direction to close the case
shall be applicable.
7. We are also informed that a coordinate Bench of this
Court in Miscellaneous Application No. 729 of 2025 in
Criminal Appeal No. 1927 of 2025 titled “Pinki Versus The
State of Uttar Pradesh and Anr.” while dealing with the
issue of human trafficking taking place through Surrogacy
and Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) clinics, and
for the proper implementation of the Assisted Reproductive
Technology  (Regulation)  Act,  2021  and  the  Surrogacy
(Regulation) Act, 2021, the present Committee headed by
Ms. Mukta Gupta, learned Senior Counsel has been entrusted
to  go  into  that  aspect  also,  and  the  report  to  be
10

--- Page 75 ---
SLP (CRL.) NO.11263/2025
submitted in the present proceedings may also have a
Chapter on such issue(s).
8. Let the same be done accordingly.
9. For integrating all portals, be it National or State,
it appears that there are some glitches. Having regard to
the aforesaid, we direct that the agencies which operate
such  portal(s)  will  sit  together  and  get  the  issue
resolved with regard to seamless integration of data from
one  platform  to  the  other  by  taking  the  help  of
specialists  in  the  field.  The  National  Crime  Records
Bureau (NCRB) shall coordinate such exercise. Substantive
progress in this regard should also be reflected in the
report to be submitted by the NCRB by the next date. We
are informed that NCRB is a participating agency. Let Ms.
Archana Pathak Dave, learned ASG communicate this order to
the NCRB for its immediate and strict compliance.
10. The Court would also indicate that the ultimate aim
should be that there is seamless transmission/integration
of data from whatever local or other digital portal which
is in existence to the CCTNS 2.0.
11. It shall not be an excuse for the CCTNS that all
Police Stations are not being digitized/computerized. The
work of the CCTNS is to ensure that there is integration
of all such platforms, which has nothing to do whether all
police  stations  or  other  institutions  are  digitized/
11

--- Page 76 ---
SLP (CRL.) NO.11263/2025
computerised.
12. In view of the Court being informed by Dr. P.M. Nair,
learned Member of the Committee, that as of now the Police
Stations are required to upload the data with them on the
CCTNS, as also on the mission Vatsalya, there should be a
software so that uploading on any one platform would
automatically  integrate  the  same  on  all  connected
platforms,  meaning  thereby  that  there  is  real  time
synchronisation, that too, by uploading of the data on any
one of the concerned platforms. 
13. The following suggestion at Paragraph No. 17(vi) of
the Third Status Report is reproduced for further clarity:
“17(vi)  Necessity  to  have  complete  and
seamless integration of information between
CCTNS and Mission Vatsalya portal, so that
there is no duplication of data entries and
there  is  real-time  update  of  information
between the two platforms. The National Crime
Records Bureau (NCRB) and Ministry of Women
and Child Development (MWCD)alongwith their
software developers are required to prepare a
common integration plan, which indicates the
present  status  of  integration  of  the  two
platforms and the exact time that would be
required  in  completing  the  remaining
integration.”
14. The  term  Police  Station  shall  include  all  such
12

--- Page 77 ---
SLP (CRL.) NO.11263/2025
institutions or stations which have the power under the
BNSS or any other relevant Statute to take action with
regard to any criminal activity, including the Railway
Police and also to all agencies which have the power to
take  cognizance  and  investigate  and  take  action  with
regard to missing persons. 
15. A suggestion has also been made at Paragraph No.17(x)
of the Third Status Report, which reads as under:
“17(x) CCTNS is also required to integrate
data from the CCTVs installed at all Railway
Stations and bus stands in India because the
major means of transportation of a person
trafficked is through buses or railways.” 
16. We find the said suggestion to be very relevant and to
add to the same, it shall also include the Airports. The
exercise  to  be  undertaken  should  also  include  the
aforesaid suggestion. In addition, since India has a very
long coastline and human trafficking has been found to be
taking place through the water route, such exercise should
also cover the ports.  
17. For the purpose of convenience, let the copies of the
Third Status Report submitted by the team headed by Ms.
Mukta Gupta, be supplied to the learned Counsel for the
States/U.Ts. through email by the learned Advocate on
Record assisting the Committee. 
13

--- Page 78 ---
SLP (CRL.) NO.11263/2025
18. We direct the concerned State Governments to wake up
to the situation and ensure that the orders passed from
time to time, especially the directions given today are
strictly complied with within the time frame indicated. 
19. The Chief Secretaries who were directed to appear and
in whose cases no exemption has been granted by the Court,
including where applications have been filed but no order
passed, were required to be physically present before the
Court today, but have chosen not to do so. In view
thereof, notice for contempt is issued against the said
Chief Secretaries. Registry to act accordingly.
20. In respect of the State of Kerala and U.T. of Daman
and Diu, though appearance has to be directed, but in view
of the fact that on earlier occasion also we had exempted
from personal appearance Chief Secretaries of the States
where the initial affidavit had been filed, the State of
Kerala and U.T. of Daman and Diu are also given that
benefit. Chief Secretaries of the State of Kerala and U.T.
of Daman and Diu stand exempted from personal appearance. 
21. We request Ms. Mukta Gupta, learned Senior Advocate,
to also take note of the suggestion made by the State of
Tamil Nadu in its report filed on 17.04.2026.
22. The Court is now taking the matter with regard to the
Commissioners of Police of Delhi and Gurugram.
23. An affidavit has been filed by the Commissioner of
14

--- Page 79 ---
SLP (CRL.) NO.11263/2025
Police, Gurugram, Mr. Shibash Kabiraj. Mr. Ayush Yadav,
DCP South, Gurugram is present in Court. However, he
submitted that he has taken charge only on 22.09.2026.
Thus, we called upon the learned Counsel for the State of
Haryana to ensure the presence of the then DCP, who
currently holds the post of DCP, Traffic, Gurugram. In
terms thereof, Mr. Hitesh Yadav, DCP Traffic, Gurugram is
also present in Court. From the affidavit filed by the
Commissioner of Police, Gurugram, we find that there has
been not one but continuous lapses/blunders committed by
the Police. We cannot accept such happening from a metro
police like Gurugram and that too, where there is a
Commissionerate,  where  more  powers  are  vested  in  the
Police than in other Districts where Superintendents of
Police head the post and in such a scenario, when a body
of a dead person is recovered and which is not identified,
the casualness with which it is treated that its details
are not uploaded on the portals concerned and then after
four  days,  the  post-mortem  is  held  and  the  body  is
cremated with whatever there was on the body like the kada
and the watch worn by the person which is proved from the
fact that the articles which have been received by the
family with regard to the last mortal remains of the
deceased, include a burnt kada and a burnt watch. There
are no answers forthcoming, either from the learned State
15

--- Page 80 ---
SLP (CRL.) NO.11263/2025
counsel or from the present and past DCPs and neither the
same is available in the affidavit of the Commissioner of
Police, Gurugram.
24. Learned counsel for the State of Haryana submitted
that  action  has  been  initiated  against  the  concerned
Investigating Officer, SHO, the Control Room Incharge and
the two Doctors, one being the Doctor who was the part of
the FSL team which went to the scene of the crime and the
other, who actually conducted the post-mortem.

1. Heard. Leave granted.
2. By the impugned order, the jurisdictional High Court has refused to
condone  the  delay  of  130  days  in  filing  two  intra-court  appeals,
namely Special Appeal Defective No. 426 of 2024 and Special Appeal
Defective No.427 of 2024, on the ground that cause for delay was not
properly explained and the cause shown was not being satisfactory.
3. We  have  heard  the  learned  advocates  appearing  for  the  parties  at
length. The short question that would arise for our consideration is:
“Whether in the facts and circumstances of the case, the
delay of 130 days ought to be condoned or the impugned
order  rejecting  the  cause  shown  as  being  insufficient,
deserves to be affirmed?”
1

--- Page 84 ---
Without going into all the details and burdening this order, it would
suffice to state that two writ petitions, namely, Writ A No.12482 of
2019  and  Writ  A  No.518  of  2024,  came  to  be  filed  by  the
respondents herein before the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad,
Lucknow  Bench,  challenging  the  office  memorandum  dated
04.07.2018  issued  by  the  U.P.  Co-operative  Federation  Limited
(hereinafter  referred  to  as  ‘Appellant’  for  sake  of  brevity  and
convenience).  The  said  writ  petitions  came  to  be  allowed  by
judgment  dated  29.02.2024.  For  non-compliance  of  the  said
judgment rendered in Writ A No.518 of 2024, Contempt Application
(C)  No.2841  of  2024  came  to  be  filed  and  by  the  order  dated
25.07.2024, notice to the contemnors, namely, the appellant herein,
came to be issued. Immediately thereafter, for non-compliance of the
judgment rendered in Writ A No.518 of 2024, Contempt Application
(C) No.3050 of 2024 came to be filed and notice came to be issued to
the contemnor, i.e., appellant herein, on 05.08.2024.
4. Against the aforesaid common judgment and order passed in Writ A
No.12482 of 2019 and Writ A No.518 of 2024, intra-court appeals
2

--- Page 85 ---
were  filed  on  07.08.2024  in  S.A.D.  No.426  of  2024  and  S.A.D.
No.427  of  2024,  along  with  an  application  for  stay  of  the  said
judgment  and  an  application  for  condonation  of  delay.  The
respondents in the said appeals were granted 10 days’ time to file
objections to the application for condonation of delay by the order
dated 14.08.2024. On 29.08.2024, the appeals came to be adjourned
to 05.09.2024 by recording that liberty is granted to the parties to
seek adjournment before the contempt court, as the Division Bench
was seized of the matter. Hence, the court adjudicating the contempt
took note of the same and ordered to list the contempt application
after  the  decision  of  the  aforesaid  special  appeal  along  with
Contempt  Application  (C)  No.  2841  of  2024.  When  Contempt
Application (C) No. 2841 of 2024 was taken up for consideration on

made by both the parties and granted three weeks’ time, since the

order is not granted in the special appeal, the respondent would file
an  affidavit  of  compliance.  The  aforesaid  appeal  was  listed  on
25.10.2024 and Division Bench of High Court took note of the fact
that  despite  the  appeal  pending,  the  contempt  proceedings  is
3

--- Page 86 ---
continuing  and  as  such  it  held  that  contempt  proceedings  would
remain  deferred  till  the  next  date  of  listing  and  accordingly
adjourned the matter to 07.11.2024. However, on passing of the said
order, the learned counsel appearing before the court brought to the

the  matter  on  next  date,  i.e.,  26.11.2024.  Again,  the  matter  was
ordered  to  be  listed  on  05.12.2024.  On  the  same  date,  i.e.,
05.12.2024, a supplementary affidavit in respect of the application
for condonation  of delay in Special  Appeal  Defective  No.427 of
4

--- Page 87 ---
2024 was also filed by the contemnor. On 19.12.2024, the contemnor
was granted six weeks’ time to file compliance affidavit and failing
which it was held that the charges would be framed.  When the
contempt application was listed on 16.01.2025 and application for
impleading the present  Managing  Director in place  of the earlier
Managing Director who had been transferred came to be filed and it
was allowed and notice were issued to the impleaded respondent to
show  cause  why  contempt  proceedings  should  not  be  initiated
against him for wilful disobedience of the order dated 29.02.2024
passed in the common judgment and Writ A No.518 of 2024 and
connected matters.
5. Being aggrieved by the same SLP (C) No.5406 of 2025 was filed
before this Court and this Court by order dated 17.03.2024 granted
stay  of  the  order  impugned,  i.e.,  16.01.2025,  vide  order  dated
17.03.2025.  Subsequently  when  the  said  SLP  was  listed  on
25.02.2026,  this  Court  by  order  dated  25.05.2026  requested  the
Division Bench of the High Court to take up and dispose of this
special appeal referred to herein supra i.e., for 426 and 427 of 2024
i.e., Special Defective Appeal and till disposal of the same contempt
proceedings came to be stayed. The Division Bench thereafter by the
5

--- Page 88 ---
impugned order, took up both the appeals and dismissed the appeals
on the ground of delay as already been noticed herein above.
6. Though the learned counsel appearing for the appellant(s) has raised
hue  and  cry  that  the  jurisdictional  High  court  was  agitated  on
account of the appellant having approached this Court, we are not
inclined  to  examine  the  said  contention  and  it  does  not  merit
consideration. Turning our attention to the core issue, namely, as to
whether appeals could have been dismissed on the ground of delay
or the delay ought to have been condoned, it requires to be noted
that,  at  the  outset  that  no  litigant  would  stand  to  benefit  by
approaching the Courts belatedly. While considering the prayer for
condonation of delay, it is not the length of delay, it is the cause for
the delay  which would be of paramount consideration.  However,
short  the  delay  may  be,  if  the  cause  shown  does  not  inspire
confidence or it is not in the proximity of truth, the cause shown for
delay cannot be accepted. Even, if the length of delay is too long and
the cause shown is sufficient, as prescribed under Section 5 of the
Limitation Act, 1963 and if it would fall within ‘sufficient cause’,
irrespective of the length of delay, same deserves to be condoned.
This  Court  has  repeatedly  held  that  certain  amount  of  latitude
6

--- Page 89 ---
requires to be extended in respect of the appeals filed by the State
where delay on account of administrative reasons would occur and if
such administrative reasons are genuine, bonafide and without any
malafide intention, such cause deserves to be condoned.  
7. At this juncture, we may note with benefit the judgment of this Court
in the case of Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag and Another  v.
Mst. Katiji and Others , reported in  AIR 1987 SC 1353: (1987) 2
SCC 107, whereunder it has been held as follows:
“3. The legislature has conferred the power to condone delay by
enacting Section 5 of the Indian Limitation Act of 1963 in order
to  enable  the  courts  to  do  substantial  justice  to  parties  by
disposing  of  matters  on  "merits".  The  expression  "sufficient
cause" employed by the legislature is adequately elastic to enable
the  courts  to  apply  the  law  in  a  meaningful  manner  which
subserves the ends of justice that being the life-purpose for the
existence of the institution of courts. It is common knowledge
that this Court has been making a justifiably liberal approach in
matters instituted in this Court. But the message does not appear
to have percolated down to all the other courts in the hierarchy.
And  such  a  liberal  approach  is  adopted  on  principle  as  it  is
realized that:
"1. Ordinarily a litigant does not stand to benefit by
lodging an appeal late.
2. Refusing  to  condone  delay  can  result  in  a
meritorious  matter  being  thrown  out  at  the  very
threshold  and  cause  of  justice  being  defeated.  As
against this when delay is condoned the highest that
can happen is that a cause would be decided on merits
after hearing the parties.
3. "Every  day's  delay  must  be  explained"  does  not
mean that a pedantic approach should be made. Why
not  every  hour's  delay,  every  second's  delay?  The
doctrine must be applied in a rational common sense
pragmatic manner.
7

--- Page 90 ---
4. When  substantial  justice  and  technical
considerations are pitted against each other, cause of
substantial justice deserves to be preferred for the other
side  cannot  claim  to  have  vested  right  in  injustice
being done because of a non-deliberate delay.
5. There is no presumption that delay is occasioned
deliberately, or on account of culpable negligence, or
on account of mala fides. A litigant does not stand to
benefit by resorting to delay. In fact he runs a serious
risk.
6. It must be grasped that judiciary is respected not on
account of its power to legalize injustice on technical
grounds  but  because  it  is  capable  of  removing
injustice and is expected to do so.
Making  a  justice-oriented  approach  from  this
perspective, there was sufficient cause for condoning
the delay in the institution of the appeal. The fact that
it was the "State" which was seeking condonation and
not  a  private  party  was  altogether  irrelevant.  The
doctrine  of  equality  before  law  demands  that  all
litigants, including the State as a litigant, are accorded
the same treatment and the law is administered in an
even-handed  manner.  There  is  no  warrant  for
according a step-motherly treatment when the "State"
is the applicant praying for condonation of delay. In
fact  experience  shows  that  on  account  of  an
impersonal machinery (no one in charge of the matter
is directly hit or hurt by the judgment sought to be
subjected  to  appeal)  and  the  inherited  bureaucratic
methodology  imbued  with  the  note-making,  file-
pushing and passing-on-the-buck ethos, delay on its
part  is  less  difficult  to  understand  though  more
difficult  to  approve.  In  any  event,  the  State  which
represents the collective cause of the community, does
not  deserve  a  litigant-non-grata  status.  The  courts
therefore  have  to  be  informed  with  the  spirit  and
philosophy  of  the  provision  in  the  course  of  the
interpretation of the expression "sufficient cause". So
also  the  same  approach  has  to  be  evidenced  in  its
application to matters at hand with the end in view to
do even-handed justice on merits in preference to the
approach which scuttles a decision on merits. Turning
to the facts of the matter giving rise to the present
appeal, we are satisfied that sufficient cause exists for
the delay. The order of the High Court dismissing the
8

--- Page 91 ---
appeal before it as time-barred, is therefore, set aside.
Delay is condoned. And the matter is remitted to the
High Court. The High Court will now dispose of the
appeal  on  merits  after  affording  reasonable
opportunity of hearing to both the sides.” 
As  noted  in  the  aforesaid  judgment,  everyday  delay  need  not  be
explained. If said yardstick is applied, then question may arise why
not every second of delay should be explained. When the officials
who man the process of filing of the appeals does not exhibit lethargy,
the cause shown for administrative delay cannot be ignored and right
cause cannot be nipped at the bud by dismissing it on the technical
ground of delay. If the cause shown is sufficient, the delay deserves to
be condoned.
8. This Court in the case of State of Nagaland v. Lipok AO and Others,
(2005) 3 SCC 752, has held as follows:
“15. It is axiomatic that decisions are taken by officers/agencies
proverbially at a slow pace and encumbered process of pushing
the  files  from  table  to  table  and  keeping  it  on  the  table  for
considerable time causing delay - intentional or otherwise - is a
routine. Considerable delay of procedural red tape in the process
of their making decision is a common feature. Therefore, certain
amount of latitude is not impermissible. If the appeals brought by
the  State  are  lost  for  such  default  no  person  is  individually
affected  but  what  in  the  ultimate  analysis  suffers,  is  public
interest. The expression "sufficient cause" should, therefore, be
considered with pragmatism in a justice-oriented approach rather
than  the  technical  detection  of  sufficient  cause  for  explaining
every  day's  delay.  The  factors  which  are  peculiar  to  and
characteristic of the functioning of the governmental conditions
would  be  cognizant  to  and  requires  adoption  of  pragmatic
approach in justice-oriented process. The court should decide the
9

--- Page 92 ---
matters on merits unless the case is hopelessly without merit. No
separate standards to determine the cause laid by the State vis-à-
vis  private  litigant  could  be  laid  to  prove  strict  standards  of
sufficient  cause.  The  Government  at  appropriate  level  should
constitute  legal  cells  to  examine  the  cases  whether  any  legal
principles  are  involved  for  decision  by  the  courts  or  whether
cases require adjustment and should authorise the officers to take
a decision or give appropriate permission for settlement. In the
event of decision to file appeal, needed prompt action should be
pursued by the officer responsible to file the appeal and he should
be made personally responsible for lapses, if any. Equally, the
State cannot be put on the same footing as an individual. The
individual would always be quick in taking the decision whether
he would pursue the remedy by way of an appeal or application
since  he  is  a  person  legally  injured  while  the  State  is  an
impersonal machinery working through its officers or servants.”
9.  Keeping  the  aforesaid  principles  in  mind,  when  we  turn  our
attention to the facts unfolded in the instant case, it would indicate
that  prime  cause  for  delay  is  on  account  of  the  administrative
constraints. It has been specifically pleaded in the affidavit filed in
support of the application for condonation of delay that competent
authority had to take a decision for filing the appeal against the order
dated 29.02.2024 and he was discharging the duties of being election
observer in the state of Gujarat in the general elections during the
period March 2024 to May 2024. It is also stated that immediately
thereafter the High Court remained closed due to summer vacation in
June 2024 and immediately after returning from the duty as observer,
the Managing Director of the appellant Federation is said to have
10

--- Page 93 ---
perused the order dated 29.02.2024 and on obtaining legal opinion
filed the appeal immediately on 26.07.2024.  The steps taken from
the date of receipt of certified copies till the date of filing of the
appeal has been explained in detail at paragraph nos.9 to 20 of the
supplementary affidavit dated 05.12.2024. Thus, it can be seen that
the Managing Director of the appellant Federation had been deputed
as an election observer for the Lok Sabha Election, 2024 and for
want  of  his  administrative  approval,  the  delay  seems  to  have
occasioned. The cause shown for the delay, thus cannot be construed
as mala fide or the said delay being intentional. To put it differently,
the cause shown being in the proximity of the truth and would fall
within  the  four  corners  of  ‘sufficient  cause’  as  envisaged  under
Section 5 of the Limitation Act, 1963 and as such the delay of 130
days  in  filing  the  appeal  ought  to  have  been  condoned.  The
impugned order dismissing the application for condonation of delay
thus cannot be sustained. On account of the writ applicants having
been per forced to appear before the High Court and before this
Court  for  opposing  the  application  for  condonation  of  delay  and
having spent both time and money, we are of the considered view
that they should be suitably compensated.
11

--- Page 94 ---
10.For reasons assigned hereinabove, we set aside the impugned order
conditionally, namely, by directing appellant(s) herein to pay costs to
each  of  the  writ  applicant  quantified  at  Rs.2000/-  (Rupees  Two
Thousand) per person, payable within an outer limit of four weeks
from today and only on production of proof of having paid the cost
or deposited the cost, the appeals shall be taken up and heard on
merits and in accordance with law. The said costs shall be deposited
before  the  jurisdictional  High  Court  or  paid  to  each  of  the  writ
applicant directly and the High Court shall adjudicate the appeal on
merits  and  in  accordance  with  law  expeditiously,  subject  to
cooperation by the learned advocates appearing for the parties and
during the pendency of the said appeal, the contempt proceedings
shall remain stayed.
11. Accordingly, these appeals stand disposed of.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand consigned to records.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
(Arising out of S.L.P.(Civil) No.5232 of 2026)
JAIPUR METRO RAIL CORPORATION  ... APPELLANT(S) 
                  VS.
CONTINENTAL ENGINEERING CORPORATION LIMITED  ... RESPONDENT(S)
                                                         
          O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. Heard  Ms.  Aishwarya  Bhati,  learned  Additional
Solicitor General appearing for the appellant and Mr.
Anil  Kher,  learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent-Corporation.
3. The  present  appeal  calls  in  question  the
correctness of the order dated 21st August, 2025 passed by
the High Court of Judicature for Rajasthan, Bench at
Jaipur, in D.B.Special Appeal (Civil) No.4 of 2022.
4. The limited grievance raised by learned Additional
Solicitor  General  is  that  the  Division  Bench,  while
relegating the adjudication of the matter, should have
left it to the learned Single Judge to decide whether the
application filed under Section 34 of the Arbitration and
1

--- Page 113 ---
Conciliation Act, 1996 (for short, “the A & C Act”)  was
entertainable, particularly, in view of the objection of
the appellant herein that it was barred time. Learned
Additional Solicitor General contends that the Division
Bench ought not to have gone into the aspect of exclusion
of time.  Paragraphs 19 to 22 of the impugned order read
as under:
“19. It is settled law that merely mentioning
a wrong heading of provision on the application
would not defeat the cause of justice.  The
contents of the application are required to be
seen and not the provision mentioned on it.
The court can understand by a bare reading of
the application as to under which provision the
same has been filed and what the litigant
(here, the appellant) means to plead before the
court.  From a perusal of the application moved
by  the  appellant  it  is  apparent  that  the
application  moved  by  the  appellant  it  is
apparent that the application filed by the
appellant  was  of  the  nature  of  raising
objections against dismissal of the award by
the Tribunal.  Thus, the Single Judge who had
been assigned specially to hear the application
on merits by the Division Bench ought to have
considered the merits of the case.
20. We also notice that it is a case where
the  respondent  has  attempted  to  delay
adjudication of the application under Section
34 of the Act of 1996 by one reason or the
2

--- Page 114 ---
other  on  technical  grounds.   Before  the
Commercial Court, the respondents themselves
have raised the question of jurisdiction and
their application was accepted by the concerned
Commercial Court, the course adopted by the
appellant cannot be faulted in filing the same
application which was returned to them by the
concerned State Commercial Court.  The contents
of the said application clearly reveal it being
objections under Section 34 of the Act of 1996
which  were  originally  filed  before  the
Commercial Court.  The learned Single Judge,
therefore,  ought  to  have  looked  into  the
contents thereof.  We are, therefore, unable to
accept the findings arrived at by the learned
Single Judge that there was no application
moved under Section 34 of the Act of 1996 by
the appellant and we, therefore, do not confirm
the same.
21. As  regards  delay  in  filing  of  the
application, we have considered the law as laid
down in M.P.Steel Corporation (supra) , taking
into consideration the fact that while Arbitral
Tribunal may not be the court in strict sense,
but the principle of law with regard to the
appellant prosecuting with due diligence need
to be looked into as per Explanation (a) to
Section 14 of the Limitation Act.  Therefore,
it is apparent that the time spent by the
appellant in pursuing the wrong forum needs to
be condoned.  Accordingly, we find that there
were sufficient reasons to ignore the delay
3

--- Page 115 ---
which has occurred in filing the application
before this court.  The forum was wrongly
chosen or legally advised and once there were
written submissions alongwith the application
under Section 14 of the Limitation Act was on
record,  the  course  which  should  have  been
adopted was to hear on the application instead
ignoring the same.  We are, therefore, left
with no option but to set aside the findings
arrived at by the learned Single Judge and
allow this appeal and set aside the order dated
02.03.2022 passed by the learned Single Judge.
22. Consequently, the appeal is allowed and
the  order  dated  02.03.2022  passed  by  the
learned Single Judge is set aside.  We remand
the matter back to the learned Single Judge
hearing  arbitration  cases  to  decide  the
application on merits.”
5. The  response  of  Mr.  Anil  Kher,  learned  senior
counsel for the respondent is that this was not a case
where the Section 34 application was barred by time, and
the only question was the applicability of the principles
analogous to Section 14 of the Limitation Act, 1963 and
that it was really a matter of exclusion of period spent
by the respondent in prosecuting  bona fide  proceedings
with due diligence before a Court without jurisdiction.
6. Learned  Additional  Solicitor  General,  however,
disputes the contention and states that even applying
4

--- Page 116 ---
Section 14 of the Limitation Act, the ingredients are not
made out and the Section 34 application is out of time.
7. We are of opinion that those are matters which
should have been left to the Single Judge to decide first
before  hearing  the  Section  34  on  merits.  Learned
Additional Solicitor General is right that only in the
event of the Single Judge excluding time and finding the
Section 34 application to be within time, that question
of consideration on merits would arise.
8. In this case, the award was passed on 20 th December,
2017 by a majority of 2:1.  On 16 th March, 2018, the
respondent  filed  an  application  being  Arbitration
Application No.29 of 2018 before the Rajasthan State
Commercial Court (District Level), Jaipur under Section
10(1) of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 (for short, ‘the
Commercial  Courts  Act,  2015’)  for  setting  aside  the
arbitral award.
9. On  22nd October,  2018,  the  appellant  filed  an
application  seeking  dismissal  of  the  Section  34
application on the ground that being an international
commercial arbitration, the appropriate fora was the High
Court of Rajasthan.
10. On 22nd November, 2018, accepting the objections of
the  respondent,  the  Commercial  Court  returned  the
5

--- Page 117 ---
application under Order VII Rule 10 of the Code of Civil
Procedure, 1908 (for short, “the CPC”) after finding that
the  arbitration  being  an  international  commercial
arbitration, the appropriate fora was the High Court of
Rajasthan.
11. On 10 th December, 2018, the respondent filed the
application before the registry of the High Court of
Judicature  for  Rajasthan,  Bench  at  Jaipur.  On  14 th
February, 2019, a fresh application under Section 10(1)
of the Commercial Courts Act, 2015 was filed before the
High Court by the respondent along with the Original
Application which was filed before the Commercial Court.
12. Learned senior counsel for the respondent clarifies
that what was filed on 14th February, 2019 was another set
of the same application, since an objection was taken
that the matter should go before the Division Bench.
13. On 2 nd February, 2022, written submissions were
filed by the respondent along with an application under
Section 14 of the Limitation Act before the High Court.
14. Learned Single Judge, on 2 nd March, 2022, dismissed
the application filed under Section 10 of the Commercial
Courts Act, 2015 holding that Commercial Court could not
have exercised power under Order VII Rule 10 of the CPC
and  it should  have rejected  the application  as not
6

--- Page 118 ---
maintainable.  Alternatively, in any event, treating the
rejection as one passed under Order VII Rule 10 of the
CPC, the respondent ought to have filed an application
under Section 4(1) of the Rajasthan Arbitration Rules,
2003 and duly verified the same.  Learned Single Judge
was  of  the  opinion  that  the  application  was  not
maintainable under Section 34 and the annexure which was
the  application  under  Section  34  filed  before  the
Commercial  Court could  not have  been treated  as an
application under Section 34 filed before the High Court.
15. Paragraph Nos. 19 and 20 of the order of the
learned Single Judge read as under:
“19. No application for extension of time was
filed  by  the  applicant.   This  Court  is
therefore of the considered view that there is
no presentation as such of any application
under Section 34 of the Act before the High
Court.  This Court is also of the considered
view that no application under Section 10(1) of
the Commercial Courts Act is required to be
filed as Section 10(1) only deals with the
jurisdiction in respect of arbitration matters.
Proper course for the applicant was to file a
fresh arbitration application or present the
arbitration  application,  which  was  returned
before the proper Officer of the Court.  No
application under Section 34 of the Act has
been filed in accordance with the Rajasthan
7

--- Page 119 ---
Arbitration Rules, thus this Court is of the
considered view that applicant is not entitled
to any relief.
20. There being no application under Section
34 of the act having been presented before a
proper Officer of the Court, there being no
application for condonation of delay, there
being no relief claimed in the application
under  Section  10(1)  with  regard  to  the
arbitration  application,  the  present
arbitration application therefore deserves to
be and is accordingly dismissed.  No orders as
to cost.”
16. Lastly, it was held that even if the application
was treated as one under Section 34 of the A & C Act, it
was  barred  by  limitation,  as  no  application  for
condonation of delay was filed.
17. On appeal against the said order, the Division
Bench has passed the impugned order. The Division Bench,
having found the application under Section 34 to have
been  rightly  filed,  however,  went  ahead  and  applied
Section 14 to exclude time and remitted the matter to the
Single Judge to consider the Section 34 application on
merits. This is how the matter presents itself before us.
18. Learned Additional Solicitor General contends that
the ingredients of Section 14 ought to have been left by
8

--- Page 120 ---
the Division Bench to the Single Judge; that notice on
Section 14 application which was filed with the written
submission, even if it was to be taken on record, ought
to  have  been  given  to  the  appellant  to  file  its
objection, and then an appropriate order excluding or not
excluding time could have been made under the principles
analogous to Section 14.
19. We find merit in this submission. Hence, while not
disturbing the remand of the matter for adjudication to
the Single Judge, we direct that the learned Single Judge
before taking up the Section 34 application should first
hear the Section 14 application after due notice to the
appellant, and only in the event of finding that after
excluding  time,  the  Section  34  application  of  the
respondent was within time, proceed to hear the matter on
merits.
20. The impugned order is modified in the above terms.
The appeal is accordingly disposed of in the above terms.
21. Considering that it is an award of 2017, we request
the learned Single Judge to make an endeavour to take up
the matter early and dispose it of at the earliest
possible.
9

--- Page 121 ---
22. All contentions are kept open.
23. There shall be no order as to costs.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The matter was listed today for the first time after we
delivered the final judgment. It has come up today to give
us  a  fair  idea,  how  the  Union  of  India  and  other
stakeholders  have  proceeded  to  comply  with  various
directions issued by us in the main judgment.
2. We dealt with a very delicate, rather a very important
and sensitive issue relating to the human trafficking of
women and children for commercial sexual exploitation. We,
in fact, provided an extensive ‘Victim Protection Plan’ for
strict adherence by all stakeholders in exercise of our
plenary powers under Article 142 of the Constitution. We had
also death with, in detail, the prayer as regards the
constitution of the Organized Crime Investigation Agency
(OCIA).  Moreover,  from  paragraphs  387  to  424,  we  had
provided certain recommendations and suggestions for serious
consideration by the Union of India.
3

--- Page 137 ---
3. Ms. Aparna Bhat, the learned senior counsel appearing
for the petitioner has provided us today with a compliance
table which identifies each and every stakeholder involved
in the implementation of the ‘Victim Protection Plan’. 
4. The stakeholders involved are as under:-
(i) All Authorities
(ii) State Governments and Departments
(iii) High Courts
(iv) Magistrates
(v) Anti Human Trafficking Units 
(vi) Rescue Teams and Leaders
(vii) NGOs and NGO Workers
(viii) Protective Homes
(ix) Social and Case Workers
(x) DLSA and Lawyers
(xi) Police Officers and Police Stations
(xii) Child Welfare Committees
(xiii) Medical and Mental Health Professionals
(xiv) Crime Records Bureau
(xv) Committees Overseeing Protective Homes
(xvi) Anti-Human Trafficking Cell
5. Thereafter, in the note, the learned senior counsel has
delineated the exact ‘Roles and Duties’ assigned to each
stakeholder under the ‘Victim Protection Plan’ in a tabular
format  and  also  indicated  the  corresponding
paragraphs/clauses from our judgment for ease of reference.
4

--- Page 138 ---
The  learned  senior  counsel  is  of  the  view  that  this
tabulation would better enable each stakeholder to grasp and
understand the nature and extent of responsibilities cast
upon them under the Victim Protection Plan.
6. The  learned  senior  counsel  has  undertaken  a  very
commendable exercise and it will go a long way in monitoring
the compliance of our directions. 
7. We also heard Ms. Aishwarya Bhati, the learned A.S.G,
appearing for the Union of India.
8. Ms. Aishwarya Bhati has provided us with a status note
highlighting what all has been done so far after the
judgment was pronounced by this Court. The note specifically
deals with the compliance of the additional directions
issued by us under paragraph 456 of the main judgment.
9. A plain reading of the status note furnished by the
learned A.S.G. reveals that the four additional directions
issued by us have not been fully complied with by all the
States/UTs, as on date. 
10. We would like to remind the all States/UTs that, (i)
notifying “recognized welfare institutions/organisations” in
accordance with the explanation to Section 15(6A) ITPA and
for the purpose of Section 17A ITPA, (ii) preparation of a
State/UT-wide list of social welfare workers eligible to
form a part of the non-official advisory board under Section
13(3)(b) ITPA and the panel maintained by the Magistrate
under Section 17(5) ITPA, (iii) designation of a Police
Nodal Officer (PNO), and (iv) designation of a Government
5

--- Page 139 ---
Nodal  Officer  (GNO),  are  absolutely  necessary  for  the
ground-level implementation of the ‘Victim Protection Plan’.
Therefore, by the next date of hearing, the Union of India
must ensure that the four additional directions as mentioned
in paragraph 456 of the main judgment are fully complied
with by all States/UTs.
11. The learned senior counsel appearing for the petitioner
has shared one copy of her compliance table today with the
learned A.S.G.
12. We are of the view that by the next date of hearing,
the Union shall call for the necessary information from all
the stakeholders referred to in the note furnished by the
learned  senior  counsel  appearing  for  the  petitioner,
inquiring, in what manner each of the directions have been
complied with and what has been done so far for meaningful
implementation of the plan which we have provided in the
judgment.
13. We take the compliance table provided to us by the
learned counsel appearing for the petitioner as well as the
status note provided to us by the learned A.S.G on behalf of
the Union of India on record.
14. At this stage, the learned senior counsel appearing for
the petitioner brought to our notice two additional aspects
that need some urgent attention. 
15. First, the learned senior counsel would submit that the
Anti-Human Trafficking Unit (ATHUs) should be given status
of a police station, in accordance with the directions
6

--- Page 140 ---
contained in Paragraph 362 b(iii) at page no.205 of the main
judgment dated 29.05.2026, at the earliest.
16. In this regard, we direct all the State/UT Governments
in their respective Home Departments to give effect to this
direction  at  the  earliest  by  issuing  an  appropriate
notification, in accordance with law.
17. The Union shall also take up this issue at the earliest
with all the States/UTs and see to it that appropriate
notifications are issued.
18. Secondly, the learned senior counsel would submit that
certain guidelines pertaining to the ‘threshold inquiry’
which is to be conducted by the Magistrate under Section 17
ITPA, are necessary. 
19. In the ‘Victim Protection Plan’, at the stage of
production of the rescued victim(s) who are adults (above
the age of 18 years) before the Magistrate under Section 17
ITPA,  we  have  incorporated  some  detailed  directions
pertaining to the conduction of a ‘threshold inquiry’ to
identify voluntary sex workers and the manner in which their
release/rehabilitation must be proceeded with. In other
words,  the  need  for  an  additional/parallel  judicial
determination to identify voluntary sex workers, by the
Magistrate, within the framework of Section 17 ITPA, was
emphasized by us. The rationale behind the need for such an
inquiry  is  provided  under  paragraphs  330-356  of  our
judgment.
20. This judicial determination takes into account various
7

--- Page 141 ---
aspects including the consent of the rescued victim and her
views on whether she wishes to be placed under long-term
safe  custody,  her  statement  about  the  voluntary/non-
voluntary nature of her work, the social worker’s assessment
of said voluntariness, whether the victim’s position is
influenced by any threats of coercion/undue influence/force,
and whether there are any safety concerns placing the victim
at real or immediate risk of danger/re-trafficking upon
release, amongst others. 
21. This threshold inquiry as regards the voluntary nature
of  the  work  of  the  rescued  victim  is  triggered
notwithstanding the opinion expressed by the rescued victim
that her work is voluntary in nature. In other words, the
magistrate  must,  under  all  circumstances,  conduct  this
threshold  inquiry  to  determine  the  further  appropriate
course of action for the protection, rehabilitation and re-
integration of the rescued victim who is an adult. 
22. The learned senior counsel appearing for the petitioner
is of the view that this process needs to be articulated
clearly and appropriate training must be imparted to the
Magistrates across the country to enable them to implement
our directions both in letter and spirit. The learned senior
counsel is also of the opinion that the creation of such
guidelines and imparting such training would ensure that the
determination process is uniform across the country. 
To that aim, we request the National Judicial Academy to
prepare a comprehensive protocol/guidelines to enable the
8

--- Page 142 ---
Magistrates to conduct this inquiry. The Petitioner may
provide assistance to the academy in the preparation of such
protocol.
23. There is one another important aspect that we wish to
address. Time and again, we have observed that, although
this Court painstakingly issues a slew of directions in the
form of guidelines or sets up a framework to ensure that the
fundamental rights of citizens are safeguarded and enforced
in reality, yet once these directions are committed to the
paper in the form of a judgment, the matter marks its abrupt
end. This Court, more often than not, has no means of
knowing whether the frameworks, guidelines or plans are
making any measurable differences in people’s lives, or what
hindrances stand in the way. The same anxiety grips us here.
We have put in place a thorough ‘Victim Protection Plan’ but
cannot tangibly ascertain whether it is having the desired
impact or faltering in its implementation. To help us gauge
this, we would like to hear from both the Petitioner and the
Union of India on how they and other involved stakeholders
can help us track progress and measure impact. 
24. By the next date of hearing, let a fresh status report
be placed on record by the Union of India. We would also
like to the petitioner to provide us a fair idea of the
progress made by the National Judicial Academy in connection
with the preparation of the aforesaid protocol/guidelines
for Magistrates. Lastly, we expect both the petitioner and
the Union to suggest concrete ways and methods that we can
9

--- Page 143 ---
adopt to track the real implementation, progress and impact
of the ‘Victim Protection Plan’. 
25. Post this matter on 14th December, 2026.
(HARPREET KAUR)                                 (POOJA SHARMA)
COURT MASTER (SH)                             COURT MASTER (NSH)

                             O R D E R
Heard learned Senior Counsel/Counsel for the parties.
2. Pursuant to the earlier order, Mr. Saurabh Gupta, IPS,
Superintendent of Police, CBI, who was entrusted with the
investigation has submitted his final report in a sealed
cover. We have perused the same. The said report be
resealed and kept on record.
3. We are not commenting on what has been stated in the
said report which will be dealt with on a later date.
4. However, we find that by and large the respondent
no.1-DLF Home Developers Ltd. appears to have discharged
its obligation under the brochure which was floated by it
while  calling  for  booking  related  to  the  project  in
question. At this point, the Court pauses to indicate that
one wall which has been constructed at one end, which is
147 meter long and 24 meter wide and was blocked for the
reason that beyond that the land had not been acquired for
making a road and it was open land belonging to private
parties, whereas on the other side, there was a gate which
provided  egress and  ingress to the residents which was
6

--- Page 150 ---
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 8049/2023
about 100 meter long and 24 meter wide which connected the
said project to the 60 feet wide Sector road. It appears
that  in  the  exercise  while  making  the  project  in
conformity with the brochure, the wall which was a dead
end, as of now, beyond which no road ever existed, has
also been demolished. From the photographs we see that
this may be a security risk.
5. Let a full wall be built by the respondent no.1-DLF
Home Developers Ltd. till the time the land beyond that is
acquired  in  accordance  with  law  for  the  purposes  of

SUNITA NAMCHOOM                            … APPELLANT
                                
VERSUS
STATE OF ARUNACHAL PRADESH & ORS.            … RESPONDENTS
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present appeal calls in question the impugned
judgment and order dated 25th September, 2024 passed in Case
No.Crl.Petn./117/2021 by the Gauhati High Court (for short,
‘the High Court’).  By the said order, the High Court has
quashed  the  First  Information  Report  being  F.I.R.
No.08/2021 dated 22 nd April, 2021, registered at P.S.:
Chongkham, District: Namasai, Arunachal Pradesh for the
offences punishable under Sections 120-B, 418 and 423 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘the IPC’) and Section
3(1)(p) of the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes
(Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 (for short, ‘the SC &
ST Act’).
3. We have heard Mr. Dushyant Verma, learned counsel
Criminal Appeal No. 4806 of 2026  1 

--- Page 154 ---
appearing for the appellant, Ms. Akansha, learned counsel
appearing for respondent No.1-State and Mr. M.L. Lahoty,
learned counsel appearing for respondent No(s). 2 and 3.
4. The F.I.R., itself, was registered by late Meohou
Namchoom who was the father of the appellant.  In the
F.I.R., respondent No(s).2 and 3 were named as accused.  It
was alleged in the F.I.R. that the complainant along with
his daughter-appellant were the owner and controller of
M/s. Chowkham Saw and Veneer Mills Pvt. Ltd. (for short,
‘the Company’).  It was, further, alleged that attempts
were being made by respondent No.2 to oust the complainant
and the appellant from their business.  It was also alleged
that the complainant was informed that respondent No.2
along with his son (respondent No.3) had on 10 th April,
2021, fraudulently and illegally sent an email from the
email account being ‘namchoom1945@gmail.com’ without his
knowledge, purportedly saying that the complainant has
resigned from the Company of which, he along with his
daughter-appellant were holding 58 per cent shares.
5. The grievance of the complainant was that when the
meeting was to be convened to induct his daughter-appellant
as the Director of the Company and when the resolution to
that effect was sought to be uploaded, it was realised that
the complainant has been logged out on account of a
Criminal Appeal No. 4806 of 2026  2 

--- Page 155 ---
resignation email sent to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs
(for short, ‘the MCA’).
6. It  is  not  in  dispute  even  before  us  that  the
investigation was at a crucial stage when the High Court,
vide the impugned judgment and order in a quash petition
filed at the behest of respondent No(s).2 and 3, had quashed
the proceedings following the principal findings. Relevant
paragraphs  of  the  impugned  judgment  and  order  are
reproduced as under:
“13. The  contents  of  the  FIR  as  extracted
hereinbefore  disclose  that  the  original
complainant and the substituted respondent no.2
are majority shareholders having 58% share in the
company. It is alleged that resignation of the
complainant from the company was fabricated and
forged. Therefore, issue relates to the office of
the Director of a private limited company. These
issues relating to management of a company are
ordinarily required to be inspected, enquired and
investigated under Chapter-XIV of the Companies
Act, 2013 and such an investigation can also be
carried out by Serious Fraud Investigation Office
as provided under the said chapter. The issues
relating to management of the affairs of the
company is not within the domain of a normal
police investigation upon lodging of an FIR.
.. .. .. .. .. .. ..
16. It is seen that the FIR was lodged on
23.04.2021 and by now three years and five months
have passed by but the IO has not filed any
charge-sheet, which leads to a presumption that
perhaps till date no evidence could be collected
of any hacking of email or illegal transmission
of resignation by email.
17. There is no material in the FIR, which
discloses any cognizable offence has been made out
Criminal Appeal No. 4806 of 2026  3 

--- Page 156 ---
because the complainant (since deceased) and the
substituted  respondent  no.2  are  still
shareholders of 58% share as stated in the FIR
and therefore, appropriate steps as permissible
under Companies Act can still be resorted to take
control of the management of the private limited
company.
.. .. .. .. .. .. ..
21. As indicated above, an offence relating to the
affairs  of  a  company  or  relating  to  dispute
regarding management of a company has to be
inspected,  enquired  and  investigated  under
Chapter-XIV of the Companies Act. The Companies
Act, 2013 being a special law prevail over the
general law. Moreover, the ingredient of cheating
as defined under Section 415 of the IPC is not
disclosed in the FIR. Moreover, the FIR does not
disclose execution of any deed of transfer of any
property  or  any  interest  therein.  Therefore,
prima facie, the ingredients of Section 418 and
423 of the IPC under which the FIR is registered
is also not disclosed in the FIR.
22.  There is no nothing on record to show that
the  petitioners  are  at  the  location  of  the
Chowkham Saw and Veneer Mills Pvt. Ltd. and they
have taken over the physical possession of the
immovable  assets  or  plant/machinery  of  the
company. Therefore, the FIR does not disclose as
to  what  was  the  conspiracy  between  the
petitioners so as to attract provision of Section
120B of the IPC.”
7. Having heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties, we are of the opinion that the High Court was not
justified in nipping the prosecution at its bud.
8. Pursuant  to  the  complaint  of  the  de-facto
complainant,  the  F.I.R.  was  registered  and  the
investigation  was  in  progress.   Clear  allegations  of
Criminal Appeal No. 4806 of 2026  4 

--- Page 157 ---
fabrication of documents were alleged.  Whether it is right
or wrong, is for the investigating agency to decipher. 
9. But, for the High Court to record a finding that these
are the issues to be ordinarily inspected and investigated
under Chapter XIV of the Companies Act, 2013 and are not
within the domain of the Police, is incorrect.  It is well
settled  that  merely  because  certain  civil  and  other
remedies are available, criminal prosecution cannot be
foreclosed. The further finding recorded by the High Court
that since a period of more than three years has elapsed
and the chargesheet has not been filed, it leads to the
presumption  that  no  evidence  could  be  collected,  is
conjectural  in  nature.   Further,  the  finding  that  no
cognizable offence was disclosed in the F.I.R. is incorrect,
and that the appellant-daughter of the de-facto complainant
is holding 58 per cent shares, are the issues not germane
to the prosecution case .  The finding that no offence has
been disclosed in the F.I.R. attracting Sections 415, 418
and 423 of the IPC, are all premature.  The F.I.R., as is
well settled, is not an encyclopedia of the prosecution
case.
10. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case,
we are of the opinion that the High Court has quashed the
Criminal Appeal No. 4806 of 2026  5 

--- Page 158 ---
proceedings at a very premature stage by applying the
principles which are alien to the quashment of proceedings
11. No arguments were advanced by the learned counsel for
the respondent(s) in support of the quash petition. 
12. For the reasons stated above, we set aside the
impugned judgment and order passed by the High Court.
Resultantly, the investigation will continue in  F.I.R.
No.08/2021 dated 22 nd April, 2021, registered at P.S.:
Chongkham, District: Namasai, Arunachal Pradesh for the
offences punishable under Sections 120-B, 418 and 423 of the
IPC and Section 3(1)(p) of the SC & ST Act.  
13. It is for the Police to decide after investigation as
to whether there is any merit in the F.I.R. or not.  The
respondent  No(s).2  and  3  are  free  to  avail  remedies
depending upon the outcome of the investigation. 
14. Needless to observe that the investigation will be
carried out uninfluenced by any of the observations made
either in the impugned judgment and order of the High Court
or in this order.
15. We make it clear that in view of the time that has
expired, in the peculiar facts of the case, respondent
No(s). 2 and 3 shall not be arrested pending investigation,
Criminal Appeal No. 4806 of 2026  6 

--- Page 159 ---
subject to their cooperation with the investigation and
furnishing bonds of Rs.25,000/- each and two sureties of
the like amount to the satisfaction of the Investigating
Officer. 
16. Accordingly, the Appeal stands allowed in the above
terms. 
17. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

O R D E R
Heard  Mr.  Shubhranshu  Padhi,  learned  counsel  for  the
appellants and Mr. Harsh Panwar, learned counsel for the respondent
No.1.
2. Leave granted.
3. The present appeal arises out of the order passed by the High
Court of Rajasthan by which the dismissal of the respondent No.1
has been interfered with and he has been directed to be reinstated
with 50% of his back wages.
4. Learned counsel for the appellants submits that appellant No.
1 is the Committee which is running a College which is totally in
the private domain, in which respondent No. 1 was initially
appointed on contractual basis for a year, which was extended
thereafter. It was submitted that despite various lapses on the
part of respondent No. 1, an opportunity was given for him to
improve, but finding that there was no improvement, a decision was
taken to terminate his services, which was in accordance with the
terms of his employment, where it was stipulated that if the
service is not satisfactory, the same may be terminated without any
notice to the employee concerned at any point of time.
5. It was further contended that the Courts below have held that
the procedure adopted by the appellants was amenable to the
stipulations  of  the  Rajasthan  Non-Government  Educational

--- Page 163 ---
3
Institutions Rules, 1993 (for short, the “Rules”) and the Rules
thereunder, especially Rule 30 which mandates that the dismissal of
a probationer can be made only with the prior approval of the
Government.
6. Learned counsel submitted that the recommendation was made for
termination and respondent No. 1 was terminated, but he fairly
admits that the approval came later inasmuch as the dismissal by
the authorities was dated 26.03.1998, whereas the approval came on
27.08.1998. It was contended that even if for the sake of argument
it is accepted that the Rules were applicable, still at best, the
consequences which may follow would be that respondent No. 1 would
be deemed to continue in service till the date of the approval by
the  Government,  which  in  actual  terms  would  mean  that  the
appellants would be liable to pay the salary for the said period.
7. It was contended that respondent No. 1 was only on probation,
and for almost the last 30 years, he has been out of service.
However, he summed up his arguments by taking a stand that the
Court may fix a lump sum amount to be paid to the respondent No. 1
in the facts and circumstances of the present case, in lieu of
reinstatement.
8. Learned counsel for respondent No. 1 submits that this is a
pure case of hostile discrimination and also of bias. It was
submitted that for no valid reason, the termination order has been
passed, and the manner in which it has been passed also shows that

--- Page 164 ---
4
the appellants do not respect any statutory provisions, though they
are bound to do so.
9. It was further contended that even the stand taken by the
appellants that the termination order could have been passed under
Rule 30, is erroneous, as, if at all, the power to terminate
exists, the same can be done only in terms of Rule 39 which relates
to all employees, irrespective of their status. It was contended
that in such view of the matter, the order passed by the High Court
needs no interference.
10. Having considered the matter in its entirety and going through
material on record, we find that the order impugned cannot be
sustained.
11. From the pleadings and whatever documents have been brought on
record, we find that the status of the respondent No. 1 remained as
a probationer. We further note that the approach of the High Court
with regard to the effect of the requirement of a prior approval
would not be fatal to the decision itself. At best, it can lead to
consequences where the employee would be deemed to be in service
till the approval is finally granted by the Competent Authority,
which in the present case is the State Government.
12. In the present case, it is not in dispute that the approval
was granted, though post facto. It is also not in dispute that the
services of respondent No. 1 were terminated w.e.f. the day the
Management passed the order. Thus, to that extent, there cannot be

--- Page 165 ---
5
any fault with the reasoning that no termination existed on the day
it was passed by the Management and the same would only become
effective from the date the Government gave approval thereto.
13. As the question of applicability of the Rules has been raised,
we find it necessary to clarify the position. Thus, we hold that in
the facts and circumstances of the present case, the matter would
be covered under Rule 30, and the consequence would be that the
effect of the termination would only be from the date on which the
approval is granted by the State Government
14. Having held that, we are now faced with a situation where
respondent No. 1 has been out of service for almost 30 years, and
may have suffered certain adverse consequences due to this position
and would thus need to be suitably compensated, particularly in the
facts and circumstances of the present case.
15. Having given our anxious thoughts to this aspect of the
matter, we find that the ends of justice would be met if the
appellants pay a sum of Rs. 5,00,000/- (Rupees Five Lakhs) as lump
sum compensation to respondent No. 1, and the matter be then
finally closed.
16. Accordingly, the appeal is allowed to the extent that the
termination of respondent No. 1 is upheld, with effect from
27.08.1998, the date on which the approval was granted by the State
Government, and further that the appellants shall pay a sum of Rs.
5,00,000/- (Rupees Five Lakhs) to respondent No. 1 within eight

--- Page 166 ---
6
weeks from today.
17. Pending applications, if any, stand disposed of.

(AHSANUDDIN AMANULLAH)
......................J.

OCTOBER 7th, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CIVIL APPEAL NO. ______ OF 2026
[SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) NO. 34584 OF 2026]
NATIONAL COMMISSION FOR INDIAN 
SYSTEM OF MEDICINE & ANR. Appellant (s)
                                VERSUS
SHIVGANGA AYURVEDIC MEDICAL COLLEGE 
AND RESEARCH CENTRE & ANR. Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. This appeal is filed against the impugned order
dated  23.09.2026  passed  by  the  High  Court  of
Judicature at Bombay, Bench at Kohlapur, in Writ
Petition No. 4686 of 2026.
3. Respondent No. 1 – College filed an application
seeking approval for 100 seats in the Undergraduate
(BAMS) course for the academic year 2024-2025.  With
effect  from  01.05.2024,  the  Minimum  Standards
Regulations came into force and the Medical Assessment
and  Rating  Board  for  Indian  System  of  Medicine,
Appellant No. 2 directed all the Institutions must
record the attendance through Biometric device called
AEBAS for students and staff.  On 30.09.2024, a Letter
of  Permission  was  granted  by  the  Appellants  to
Respondent No. 1 – College for the academic year 2024-

--- Page 205 ---
2
2025.
4. Appellant No. 2 had set the deadline for all the
Institutions to comply with the Minimum Standards of
Regulations on 18.02.2025. On inspection, Appellant
No.2 found that there were certain deficiencies in the
infrastructural facilities provided by Respondent No.
1, particularly those relating to non-implementation
of Biometric Attendance requirements.
5. On  03.12.2025,  Appellant  started  process  for
enabling the Part I Visitation Proforma for the AY
2026-2027. In furtherance of Respondents’ application
for approval of 100 seats of Undergraduate (BAMS)
course for the academic year 2026-2027, an inspection
was conducted on 27.03.2026 and after finding certain
deficiencies,  a  hearing  notice  was  issued  on
09.04.2026.
6. The enquiry process culminated in the passing of
three  orders,  being  04.09.2026,  09.09.2026  and
16.09.2026.  After  hearing  the  Respondents,
Appellant(s) imposed a fine of Rs. 1 Crore on the
college  and  levied  Rs.  1.5  Lakhs  on  every
faculty/teacher who were only present on paper, but
absent physically and also directed their suspension.
The  Respondents’  request  for  100  seats  in  the
Undergraduate (BAMS) Course for the academic year
2026-2027 was denied.

--- Page 206 ---
3
7. Challenging  the  above-referred  three  orders,
Respondent No. 1 filed a writ petition before the High
Court.
8. By the order impugned before us, the High Court
allowed the writ petition directing:-
“(A) Both the impugned orders are quashed
and set aside and substituted by following
order :-
(1) The petitioner shall pay penalty of
Rs.25,00,000/- to the respondent no.1 -
Commission within a period of two weeks.
No further time shall be granted.
(ii)  The  petitioner  shall  remove  the
deficiencies or the shortfall which are
referred  above  or  if  so  indicated
independently  by  the  respondent
authorities  to  the  petitioner  by
31.12.2026. The compliance report thereof
shall be submitted to the respondents.
(iii) The respondents shall be at liberty
to inspect / verify the petitioner college
as well as consider the compliance report.
(iv)  The  petitioner  is  permitted  to
participate in further round of admission
process and to have their teachers code
restored  for  19  faculties,  subject  to
compliance of above order and the norms or
the regulation operating in the field.”
9. Except for the directions, there is actually no
discussion about the circumstances which compelled the
High Court to pass the order.  Ms. Archana Pathak
Dave, learned Additional Solicitor General, submits
that the Appellants were also not given a proper

--- Page 207 ---
4
opportunity to contest the pleas raised in the writ
petition.  Be that as it may, it is evident from the
judgment itself that the High Court has not examined
the matter in detail and has shown undue anxiety to
dispose of the writ petition by passing the above-
referred directions.
10. While we are not in agreement with the method and
manner of disposal of the writ petition, we are not
inclined to express any opinion on the merits of the
case as we intend only to set aside the impugned order
and restore the writ petition for proper adjudication
and determination after hearing all the contesting
parties. 
11. In view of the above, the impugned order passed
by the High Court is set aside. Writ Petition No. 4686
of 2026 is restored to its original number. High Court
will now hear the contest of parties and decide the

         UPON hearing the counsel, the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The additional affidavit dated 09.10.2026 is taken on record.
We find that the 18 th Meeting of the Monitoring Committee was
held on 08.09.2026 at Kartavya Bhavan, New Delhi. 
2. However, it is distressing to note that out of the Committee
Members, only three attended the meeting physically and even
those, who were stationed in Delhi, including two Under
Secretaries to the Government, participated in the meeting
4

--- Page 221 ---
W.P.(C) No. 53/2015
through video-conferencing. 
3. We are of the opinion that those who are at least available in
Delhi should take the trouble to attend the meetings in person
as doing so online would not impart the same sense of
seriousness or focus as would be demonstrated if all such
persons  attend  the  meeting  physically.  Unless  there  are
pressing concerns which prevent those stationed in Delhi from
attending the meeting physically, they should attend the
meeting  physically  only.  Only  those  officials  who  are
stationed outside Delhi would be at liberty to participate in
such meetings online.  
4. Further, we may note that in terms of the earlier order dated
17.02.2026, meetings of the Monitoring Committee must be held
at least once in three months but if need arises, such
meetings can be held even earlier. As the last meeting was
held on 08.09.2026, we would expect the meeting to be held
before 08.12.2026, but we find that the minutes of the last
meeting leave the date open by merely stating that the next
meeting would be held in the first week of December, 2026. It
would be advisable to fix the actual date of the next meeting
as per the convenience of the committee members to obviate the
possibility of absences. 
5. All issues that were left open shall be taken up in right
earnest and addressed with all seriousness during the next
meeting. 
5

--- Page 222 ---
W.P.(C) No. 53/2015
6. We may also note that some of the complaints received from
persons hailing from North-East India could not be acted upon
for the reason that details of such complainants were not
obtained immediately and, thereafter, the authorities were not
in a position to follow up on such complaints. Henceforth,
measures shall be put in place to immediately record the full
details, including addresses, of the complainants as and when
complaints  of  any  harassment  are  received  and  necessary
further action shall be initiated without fail.
7. The Committee shall also address the issue of necessary
changes being made in the law to ensure protection and make
suitable recommendations to the authorities concerned after
due consideration. 
8. Re-list on 18.12.2026.
