05.08.2025.
2.  In the applications, the following reliefs have been prayed
for:-
“a) Clarify that the order dated 05.08.2025 passed
in Special Leave Petition (Civil) Nos. 18578-18579
2

--- Page 225 ---
M. A. Nos.  2256-2257/2026
of 2025 required the learned Arbitrator to decide
the questions referred therein at the preliminary
stage  itself  and  not  at  the  stage  of  final
bearing / award; and 
b) Clarify that the order dated 05.08.2025 passed
in Special Leave Petition (Civil) No. 18578-18579
of 2025 required the learned Arbitrator to decide
the  questions  in  the  context  of  the
Applicant/Petitioner's assertions in Special Leave
Petition (Civil) No. 18578-18579 of 2025 and not
merely on the basis of the SOC filed by Respondent
No. 1”
3. We heard Mr. Kapil Sibal and Mr. Nakul Dewan, the learned
Senior counsel appearing for the applicant/original petitioner,
and on the other hand, Mr. Neeraj Kishan Kaul, the learned
Senior counsel appearing for the opponent (original respondent
no.1). 
4. By our order dated 05.08.2025, we had requested the learned
Arbitrator to look into the four questions formulated by us as
contained in paragraph 4 of the order, referred to above. 
5. We also clarified in our order that we had nothing to say or
there  was  no  good  reason  to  interfere  insofar  as  the
appointment  of  the  Arbitrator  was  concerned.  However,  we
requested the learned Arbitrator to first hear the parties on
four questions of law formulated by us and based on the answers
proceed further accordingly.
6. To put it briefly,  prima facie,  the entire controversy
revolves around whether the Trust has stood extinguished or
3

--- Page 226 ---
M. A. Nos.  2256-2257/2026
not. It appears that in due deference to the order passed by
this Court, referred to above, the learned Arbitrator heard the
parties and has passed an order dated 08.05.2026 with which the
applicant is aggrieved, and in such circumstances, he is here
before us seeking appropriate clarification. 
7. According  to  Mr.  Sibal  and  Mr.  Dewan,  the  learned
Arbitrator has not gone by the order passed by this Court and
has still left the issue, as regards extinguishment of Trust,
open to be looked into at the stage of final hearing, more
particularly, after the statement of defence comes on record. 
8. It is needless to clarify that the client of Mr. Kaul is the
claimants & on the other hand, the client of Mr. Sibal and
Mr. Dewan is the respondent. 
9. We looked into the order passed by the learned Arbitrator. 
10. In paragraph 52 of the order dated 08.05.2026, the learned
Arbitrator has observed as under:-
“52……...The question of the existence of the Trust in
this  case  arises  only  because  the  Respondents  have
contended that it stood extinguished……..”
 
11.  After  observing  as  aforesaid,  the  learned  Arbitrator
proceeded to observe the following in paragraph 53:-
“53. The question therefore is whether the jurisdiction of
the Arbitral Tribunal can be even on the basis of a defence
raised by a Respondent.”
4

--- Page 227 ---
M. A. Nos.  2256-2257/2026
12. At the end of the order, the learned Arbitrator has
observed in paragraph 76 as under : –
“Considering the manner in which the application has
been dealt with on behalf of the Respondents, question
(a) is answered as follows;
The claim is arbitrable and maintainable. Whether the
Arbitral Tribunal has the jurisdiction to consider the
defenses relating to the extinguishment of the Trust is
kept open and all the rights and contentions of the
Claimant and the Respondents in regard thereto are kept
open and will be decided in the Award.
RE : Issue (b)
Whether the issue of extinguishment of a trust had a
direct bearing on the threshold maintainability of the
Section 11 Application filed by Respondent No. 17.”
13. What we have been able to understand from the aforesaid is
that the learned Arbitrator wants the statement of defence to
come on record for meaningful and better adjudication of the
pivotal question as regards extinguishment of the Trust. If
that be so, we direct the applicant before us to file his
statement of defence with all documents, he proposes to rely
upon, before the learned Arbitrator within a period of four
weeks from today. One set of the entire statement of defence
shall be furnished to the other side. Once the statement of
defence comes on record, we request the learned Arbitrator to
look into the same, hear both the sides and give a specific
5

--- Page 228 ---
M. A. Nos.  2256-2257/2026
finding as regards whether the Trust has stood extinguished or
is still in operation. In  other  words,  the  four  questions
which we have formulated as referred to above.
14. If ultimately, the learned Arbitrator records a finding
that the Trust has not stood extinguished, the Arbitrator shall
proceed further to decide other arbitral issues in accordance
with law.
15. If the Arbitrator records a finding that the Trust has
stood  extinguished,  he  may  pass  an  appropriate  order  in
accordance with law. 
16. At this stage, Mr. Kaul, would submit that he has some
reservations when this Court says that the only controversy is
with regard to extinguishment of Trust. According to him, the
core issue is with respect to SHA. It goes without saying that
this is a matter, which the learned Arbitrator will look into
it.
17. With the aforesaid, the Miscellaneous applications stand
disposed of.
18. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
   CIVIL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
   (Arising out of SLP(C) No.2793 of 2026)
                              
MANOJ                            APPELLANT
                                VERSUS
SUSHMABAI & ANR.                         RESPONDENTS
R1 : SUSHMABAI
R2 : IFFCO TOKIO GENERAL INSURANCE COMPANY LTD.
O R D E R
Heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. Leave granted. 
3. The present appeal arises out of the impugned order dated
11.03.2025 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur
in Misc. Appeal No.5927 of 2024, by which the appeal filed by the
appellant, who is the owner and driver of the offending vehicle,
against the award dated 15.09.2023 passed by the Second Member,
Motor Accident Claims Tribunal, Khandwa, Madhya Pradesh (for
short, the “MACT”) in MACC/261/2022 fastening liability on him
while exonerating the respondent no.2-Insurance Company to pay the
compensation amount of Rs.9,94,056/- (Rupees Nine Lakhs Ninety
Four Thousand Fifty Six) to the respondent no.1-claimant along
with interest @6 per cent per annum, has been dismissed.

--- Page 248 ---
2
4. Learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the core
issue, which the Court is required to go into is as to whether the
insurance policy covered a person other than the driver on the
vehicle, who has met with an accident. It was contented that from
the Registration Certificate Book of the vehicle, it is clear that
the  seating  capacity  is  1+1.  Thus,  the  contention  of  the
respondent  no.2-Insurance  Company  that  the  insurance  policy
covered only one person, which would mean the driver alone and
fastening the liability on the appellant, was not proper. Learned
counsel for the appellant submitted that from bare perusal of the
insurance policy though the endorsement is that the seating
capacity was one but the same column indicates that it was as per
the Registration Certificate Book, which is factually incorrect
for the reason that the Registration Certificate Book indisputedly
records that the seating capacity was 1+1. It was contented that
the insurance policy is done after looking at the Registration
Certificate Book and being satisfied that the vehicle is fit to be
insured, an insurance policy is granted by the respondent no.2-
Insurance Company and in the present case, even if there has been
a recording with regard to the seating capacity of being one, the
same being factually incorrect, the liability for the same cannot
be fastened on the appellant, who in good faith had produced the
Registration Certificate Book before the respondent no.2-Insurance
Company for insuring the vehicle in question. It was further
contented  that  in  the  present  case,  the  other  person  was
travelling on the tractor and upon falling down from the tractor,
his head came under the wheels of the tractor itself. Thus,

--- Page 249 ---
3
according to the learned counsel for the appellant, the chain of
events are complete inasmuch as, the cause of the accident was the
vehicle and the deceased was travelling on the vehicle and the
death also occurred due to the vehicle itself. It was contended
that in such view of the matter, taking a technical view with
regard to a beneficial legislation regarding insurance, where a
common man is protected for any adverse circumstances, which may
befall him or her in future and paying a premium for the same, on
such technicalities that too which are not supported by facts, the
Court may interfere and not fasten the liability for payment on
the appellant.
5. Learned counsel for the respondent no.2-Insurance Company
submitted that the insurance policy was not meant for the person,
who was travelling i.e., the deceased as he was not a conductor or
a driver and the vehicle was not a commercial vehicle.
6.  This Court is of the view that the issue of  deceased not
being  a conductor or driver does not arise as it was never in
dispute that the tractor is not a commercial vehicle in the sense
that it will have a conductor on it. Be that as it may, we have
considered the matter from various angles and find that a case for
interference has been made out.
7. As has rightly been pointed out by learned counsel for the
appellant,  there  cannot  be  a  very  strict  or  technical
interpretation on various stipulations in the insurance policy
especially with regard to what may actually have been recorded in
the insurance cover i.e., the document itself. 
8. When it is not in dispute that the Registration Certificate

--- Page 250 ---
4
Book relating to the vehicle indicates that the seating capacity
was 1+1, the mere fact that in the insurance policy, the seating
capacity is recorded as one, cannot be said to be correct more so
for the reason that it also indicates in the insurance policy that
such figure is on the basis of the Registration Certificate Book.
Further, we find that there being a direct nexus of the deceased
being seated on the tractor and falling from it and then his head
coming under the wheels of the tractor itself, the chain of events
is complete to indicate that the accident was caused by the
vehicle. The fact that the insurance was required to be covered at
least for the number of persons as indicated in the Registration
Certificate Book more so, when it deals with the tractor and not
with regard to any private transport vehicle or a commercial
vehicle, where the owner is more choosy and specific and may take
a considered view with regard to the number of persons, he or she
may get insured, we find in the present case, the deceased would
be deemed to be covered under the insurance policy in the facts
and circumstances of the present case.
9. For reasons aforesaid and on the short point, the appeal is
allowed in the peculiar facts of the present case. The award dated
15.09.2023 passed by the MACT in MACC/261/2022 as affirmed by the
High  Court,  is  modified  to  the  extent  that  the  amount  of
compensation as awarded by the MACT i.e., Rs.9,94,056/- (Rupees
Nine Lakhs Ninety Four Thousand Fifty Six) along with the interest
@6  per  cent  per  annum  to  the  respondent  no.1-claimant  is
maintained but fastening the liability on the appellant is set
aside. The amount of compensation shall be paid by the respondent

--- Page 251 ---
5
no.2-Insurance Company to the respondent no.1-claimant.
10.  Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

KRISHNA JEEVAN PANDEY      APPELLANT(S)

THE STATE OF JHARKHAND     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned counsel for the respondent-State of Jharkhand.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 25.02.2026
passed by the High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi (briefly
the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the application
filed by the appellant for suspension of sentence and
grant of bail during pendency of the appeal before the
High Court.
4. Appellant was convicted by the Special Judge, POCSO
Court, Dhanbad in Spl. (POCSO) Case No.79/2024 under
Section 376(2)(n) of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for
short, ‘IPC’) read with Section 6 of the Protection of
Children from Sexual Offences Act, 2012 (for short, ‘POCSO
Act’). Vide the judgment and order dated 19.12.2024,
1

--- Page 260 ---
appellant was sentenced to undergo Rigorous Imprisonment
(for  short,  ‘RI’)  for  20  years  along  with  fine  of
Rs.10,000/- for the offence under Section 6 of the POCSO
Act.
5. Aggrieved by the aforesaid conviction and sentence,
appellant has preferred an appeal before the High Court
which has been registered as Criminal Appeal (DB) No.673
of 2025. During the pendency of the appeal, appellant also
filed I.A. NO.606/2026, praying for suspension of the
sentence and for grant of bail which was rejected by the
High Court vide the impugned order.
6. This  Court  had  issued  notice  vide  order  dated
25.08.2026,  pursuant  to  which  respondent-State  of
Jharkhand has filed counter-affidavit.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that the
alleged incident had taken place on 02.06.2023 but the FIR
was lodged almost one year thereafter, that too by the
mother of the so-called victim on 28.05.2024. Though the
High Court had relied upon Instagram posts and Whatsapp
messages to justify rejection of the application for
suspension of sentence, he submits that appellant was not
charged for violation of any provisions of the Information
Technology Act, 2000. Further submission is that though
the High Court held the so-called victim to be a minor
based on entry made in the School Admission Register, the
deposition of Dr. Shobha Kumari disclosed that the victim
did not suffer any internal or external injury. Further,
2

--- Page 261 ---
based on radiological examination, the age of the victim
girl was assessed to be more than 18 years of age.
8. Per contra, learned counsel for the respondent-State
of Jharkhand submits that the School Admission Register
was based on the birth certificate of the victim which
clearly shows that she was a minor (aged about 16 years)
on the date of the occurrence. Therefore, no reliance can
be placed on the radiological examination of the victim
girl. Further, the allegation against the appellant is not
of a single incident, it is about continuous sexual
exploitation of the victim girl. Referring to the decision
of this Court in Kishori Lal versus Rupa, [(2004) 7 SCC
638], she submits that the High Court has given cogent
reasons while rejecting the prayer for suspension of
sentence. According to her, appellant is undergoing a
fixed sentence and has undergone only a period of 02 years
in the custody. At this stage, his sentence should not be
suspended. Instead, the High Court should be requested to
expedite the hearing of the appeal.
9. Submissions made by learned counsel for the parties
have received the due consideration of the Court.
10. At the outset, we may refer to the deposition of the
victim girl. If her deposition is considered in its
entirety, more particularly paragraph 16 onwards, a prima
facie view can be taken that there was a consensual
relationship between the appellant and the victim girl.
This  would  be  borne  out  by  her  statements  made  in
3

--- Page 262 ---
paragraphs 31 and 32 of her deposition. We have also
carefully considered the evidence of the Doctor (P.W.6)
who gave a clear opinion in her evidence that the age of
the victim girl was more than 18 years.
11. To what extent the testimony of the Doctor should be
given weightage, viz-a-viz, the School Admission Register,
is a matter to be considered by the appellate court. At
this stage, we are, prima facie, of the view that during
pendency of the appeal, appellant should be released on
bail.
12. That being the position, t he impugned order dated
25.02.2026 passed by the High Court is set aside.
13. Consequently, the sentence imposed on the appellant
stands suspended during pendency of the appeal before the
High Court and the appellant shall be released on bail on
usual terms and conditions.
14. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 (Cr.P.C.),
namely, Crl. Misc. No. 377 of 2024, Crl. Misc. No. 719 of 2024
and  Crl.  Misc.  No.  723  of  2024,  have  been  disposed  of  by
reducing  the  cost  to  50%  of  the  cost  imposed  by  learned
Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (Special Acts), Central
District, Tis Hazari Courts, Delhi vide his order dated 25th March,
2023,  whereby  the  application  made  by  the  appellant  under
Section 311 Cr.P.C. seeking permission to summon and examine
one prosecution witness and also for placing on record certain
1

--- Page 266 ---
additional documents was allowed subject to payment to cost of
Rs. 1,00,000/- by the appellant in each case.
4. Three complaint cases under Section 276C(1) of the Income Tax
Act, 1961 were lodged by the Income Tax Department against the
respondent.  An  application  under  Section  311,  Cr.P.C.  was
moved by the appellant with the prayer to summon and examine
one complainant witness and also for taking on record certain
additional documents. The application moved under Section 311,
Cr.P.C., by the department was though allowed by the learned
Magistrate by his order dated 25 th March, 2023, however, cost
was imposed to the tune of Rs. 1,00,000/- in each case.
5. The order of the learned Magistrate to the extent it imposes cost
was  challenged  by  the  appellant/department,  by  instituting
revision petitions which were dismissed being not maintainable
by the learned Additional Sessions Judge concerned, holding that
the order of the Magistrate whereby application under Section
311, Cr.P.C. was allowed, was interlocutory in nature.
6. The appellant/department  thereafter  instituted aforementioned
three  criminal  miscellaneous  petitions  under  Section  482
Cr.P.C., which have been disposed of by the High Court of Delhi
vide  order  dated  28th August,  2024,  whereby  cost  has  been
reduced to 50%. This order dated 28 th August, 2024 passed by
the High Court is under challenge.
7. Having heard the learned counsel for the parties and perused the
record available before us we are of the opinion that once the
learned Magistrate found substance in the application made by
2

--- Page 267 ---
the  appellant/department  under  Section  311  Cr.P.C.,  and
allowed the same, cost, in the facts of the case, could not have
been imposed.
8. Section 311 of the Cr.P.C. is in two parts. The first part vests the
discretion  in the  Court concerned  to  summon  any  person  in
witness or to examine any person in attendance or recall or re-
examine  any  person  already  examined,  at  any  stage  of  the
inquiry,  trial  or  proceedings  under  the  Code  of  Criminal
Procedure. The second part of Section 311 casts a duty on the
Court  concerned  to  summon  and  examine  or  recall  and  re-
examine any person if the evidence appears to it to be essential
to the just decision of the case.
9. In  the  case  of  Zahira Habibulla H. Sheikh  Versus State  of
Gujarat, (2004) 4 SCC 158 , this Court has underscored the
object of the provision contained in Section 311 Cr.P.C. and has
observed that “….Object of this Section is to enable the Court
to  arrive  at  the  truth  irrespective  of  the  fact  that  the
prosecution  or  the  defence  has  failed  to  produce  some
evidence which is necessary for a just and proper disposal
of the case. The power  is exercised  and  the evidence  is
examined neither to help the prosecution nor the defence, if
the Court feels that there is necessity to act in terms of
Section 311 but only to subserve the cause of justice and
public  interest.  It  is  done  with  an  object  of  getting  the
evidence in aid of a just decision and to uphold the truth.”
10. Accordingly, once the learned Magistrate while passing the order
3

--- Page 268 ---
dated 25 th March, 2023 has found that the documents which
were sought to be taken on record were necessary documents for
deciding the facts in issue and further that once the documents
are ordered to be taken on record then it would be a travesty of
justice if the same are not allowed to be proved, in our opinion,
imposition of cost appears to be unnecessary.
11. For the aforesaid reasons, the appeals are allowed and the orders
dated 28 th August, 2024 and 25 th March, 2023 passed by the
High  Court  of  Delhi  and  the  learned  Magistrate  concerned
respectively, so far as they  impose cost on  the appellant are
hereby set aside.

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. The instant petition has been filed under Article 32 of the
Constitution  seeking  quashing  of  FIR  No.  678  of  2026  and
consequential protection from arrest.
2. The petitioner is stated to be an investigative journalist
operating the digital news platform “Top Secret”. In the course of
1

--- Page 272 ---
his investigative journalism, he is stated to have published a
series of reports in June 2026 concerning alleged misappropriation
of offerings and other irregularities at the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi
Temple, Ayodhya. Thereafter, the subject FIR has been registered
against  him  at  P.S.  Indirapuram,  Ghaziabad,  inter-alia,
highlighting  an  incident  that  took  place  near  Shipra  Mall,
Ghaziabad, on 18.08.2026, when the petitioner, while returning
after taking his minor daughter from school, is alleged to have
struck his car in the complainant's motorcycle from behind. The
petitioner also allegedly abused and threatened the complainant and
made remarks after inquiring about his name and caste.
3. The petitioner has denied any such incident and alleges that
the occurrence was staged only because of his reporting, a brief
reference to which has already been made.
4. We may hasten to add that a copy of FIR No. 678 of 2026 was
also not supplied to the petitioner.
5. It was in this backdrop that on 25.08.2026, when the matter
came up for hearing, the following order was passed:
“1. Issue notice, returnable on 07.09.2026.
2. Dasti, in addition, is permitted. Liberty is granted
to serve the State through the Standing Counsel as well.
3. Meanwhile, no coercive action shall be taken against
the petitioner in the FIR No. 678/2026, registered at
Police Station Indirapuram, Commissionerate Ghaziabad, or
in any such subsequent FIR(s) that may be registered
against him in relation to the subject-allegations.
4. Similarly, let a copy of FIR No.678/2026 be supplied
to the petitioner, so as to enable him to avail the legal
remedy against such in FIR, in accordance with law.
2

--- Page 273 ---
5. The Commissioner of Police, Ghaziabad, shall file a
compliance affidavit in this regard.
6. As soon as a copy of the FIR is received by the
petitioner, he shall be at liberty to approach the
jurisdictional  High  Court  for  seeking  the  relevant
relief(s).”
6. In deference to the above-stated order, a copy of the FIR has
been supplied to the petitioner.
7. Meanwhile, the petitioner was able to lay his hands on a
notice dated 22.08.2026, issued to X (formerly Twitter), asking the
intermediary to furnish the digital information for a period of
three months before the registration of the subject FIR. That
notice prompted the petitioner to file IA No. 264132 of 2026,
seeking some interim-cum-final directions:
“a.Ad-Interim,  ex-parte  Stay  the  operation,
implementation and effect of the notice dated 22.08.2026
issued by the Crime Branch Investigation Unit, Ghaziabad,
in connection with FIR No.0678/2026, and restrain the
Respondents  from  seeking,  obtaining,  accessing,
processing  or  disclosing  any  information  pursuant
thereto, including the digital/account information of the
Petitioner’s X account @upadhyayabhii; AND further be
pleased to Quash the impugned notice dated 22.08.2026
issued by the Crime Branch Investigation Unit, Ghaziabad,
b. Pass such other or further order(s) as this Hon’ble
Court  may  deem  fit  and  proper  in  the  facts  and
circumstances of the present case.”
8. In the consequential affidavit, filed by the Commissioner of
Police, Ghaziabad, it is stated that after the registration of the
FIR on 20.08.2026, efforts were made to locate the petitioner on
20-22.08.2026,  but  he  could  not  be  traced.  Thereafter,  the
3

--- Page 274 ---
offending notice was issued to the nodal officer of ‘X’ for the
limited  purpose  of  tracing  the  petitioner's  whereabouts  and
facilitating arrest/investigation.
9. It is also averred that in view of our interim order dated
25.08.2026, the purpose of tracing the petitioner has become
irrelevant.
10. On the issue re: whether the investigating agencies could seek
digital information/personal information of the petitioner, even
for a period prior to three months of the registration of the FIR,
the  petitioner  has  disputed  the  clarification  given  by  the
Commissioner of Police, Ghaziabad and has prayed for a direction to
the Respondents to file a fresh, specific compliance affidavit,
addressing the issue on production of notice under Section 94 of
the BNSS.
11. We find that the impugned notice dated 22.08.2026, commanding
‘X’ to furnish petitioner's account’s log-in IP, log-out IP,
alternative email ID, mobile number, location access (latitude and
longitude),  mobile  device,  IMEI  number,  name,  address,  phone
number, registration IP logs, and IP access logs details from
01.06.2026 to 22.08.2026 pertain to a period that largely is prior
to the date of the alleged road-rage incident.
12. It may thus be seen that the explanation given by the
Commissioner  of  Police,  Ghaziabad,  in  his  affidavit  that
information was sought primarily to trace and arrest the petitioner
is  in  contradiction  with  the  contents  of  the  notice  dated
22.08.2026. Be that as it may and considering the circumstances of
this  case,  no  confidential  or  personal  information  of  the
4

--- Page 275 ---
petitioner can be obtained for the period prior to the date of
offence. Even information pertaining to the period after the
registration of the FIR cannot be sought unless adequate measures
are in place to preserve the privacy of personal data and ensure
the  principles  of  proportionality  are  applied,  i.e.,  when
alternative  measures  to  take  the  investigation  to  a  logical
conclusion are found inadequate. No such plea has been raised on
behalf of the respondents. The case being so, the notice dated
22.08.2026 issued by the local police to ‘X’ is hereby quashed. Any
information taken pursuant thereto or otherwise, shall not be
utilised against the petitioner.
13. This court, while issuing notice on 07.09.2026 has already
directed that no coercive action shall be taken against the
petitioner. In view of his voluntary statement, he will cooperate
with the ongoing investigation. That being so, the order dated
25.08.2026,  read  with  the  order  dated  07.09.2026,  are  made
absolute. The arrest of the petitioner shall remain stayed until
further orders.
14. Since a copy of the FIR has now been supplied to the
petitioner, he shall be at liberty to challenge the same before the
jurisdictional High Court in accordance with law.
15. The petitioner shall also be at liberty to approach the Court
of competent jurisdiction, in appropriate proceedings, to lay down
mandatory guidelines for the purpose of collection of personal data
and provide digital data in the course of an investigation.
Meanwhile, the restriction imposed in paragraph 12 of this order
shall continue in force.
5

--- Page 276 ---
16. We are further informed that the petitioner's vehicle has been
seized during the course of investigation. Let the same be released
forthwith and not later than two days.
17. Since we have not expressed our opinion with respect to the
contents of the FIR, all the grounds to challenge the same are
available to the petitioner. The Writ Petition and the I.A.s are
disposed of, in the above terms.
18. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand closed.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.                 OF 2026
[@ Diary No.63595 of 2025]
SUMER INTERNATIONAL LIMITED                   … APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
ORIENTAL INSURANCE CO LTD        … RESPONDENT(S)
                             
O R D E R
Delay condoned. 
2. The present Civil Appeal arises out of the judgment and order dated
18.08.2025  passed  by  the  National  Consumer  Disputes  Redressal
Commission, New Delhi (hereinafter referred to as the “NCDRC”) in OP
No. 73 of 2003, whereby the complaint filed by the appellant was allowed
in part, directing the respondent - insurance company to pay a sum of
Rs.65,36,450/-  along  with  interest  at  the  rate  of  6%  per  annum  from
28.02.2003 being the date of filing of the complaint, till the date of actual
payment.
3. The learned counsel for the appellant submitted that the appellant
had  obtained  a  Standard  Fire  Policy  from  the  respondent  -  insurance
company for the period from 01.05.2000 to 30.04.2001. On 02.01.2001 at
about 2.30 a.m., a fire broke out at the appellant’s premises, engulfing the
1

--- Page 278 ---
entire packaging section. The respondent repudiated the insurance claim.
Aggrieved thereby, the appellant preferred a complaint before the NCDRC,
seeking indemnification of Rs. 99,90,000/- along with interest at the rate of
18% per annum from the date of filing of the complaint till realisation. The
NCDRC, however, awarded a sum of Rs.65,36,450/- along with interest at
the rate of 6% per annum. 
4. The  learned  counsel  further  submitted  that  the  appellant  has
confined the present appeal to the rate of interest awarded by the NCDRC.
It was contended that the award of interest at 6% per annum results in
unjust enrichment of the respondent, which has wrongfully retained and
utilised the amount payable under the insurance claim for over two decades.
It was urged that such a rate fails to serve the restitutive purpose of interest
and  to  deter  institutional  delays  in  settling  legitimate  insurance  claims.
Reliance was also placed on earlier decisions of this Court wherein interest
at the rate of 12% per annum was awarded in comparable cases involving
delayed  payment  of  insurance  indemnity.  It  was  submitted  that  the
appellant had suffered considerable financial hardship, loss of business and
investment opportunities during the prolonged period of litigation and that
interest  at  6%  per  annum  was  therefore  inadequate  and  warranted
enhancement. 
5. Per  contra,  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the  respondent  -
2

--- Page 279 ---
insurance company submitted that there is no mandatory rule requiring the
award of interest at the rate of 12% per annum in every case involving
delayed payment. It was contended that the rate of interest is discretionary
and must be determined having regard to the facts and circumstances of
each  case  and  the  prevailing  economic  conditions.  Therefore,  it  was
submitted that the rate of interest at 6% per annum awarded by the NCDRC
was  fair  and  reasonable  and  consistent  with  the  applicable  judicial
principles. 
6. We have considered the rival submissions and perused the material
placed on record. 
7. There is no dispute between the parties with regard to the quantum
of  compensation  awarded  by  the  NCDRC.  The  sole  grievance  of  the
appellant  is  that  the  interest  awarded  at  the  rate  of  6%  per  annum  is
inadequate  and  warrants  enhancement  to  12%  per  annum,  whereas  the
respondent  maintains that the rate  awarded by the NCDRC  is just and
reasonable and does not call for interference.
8. Both parties have relied upon judicial precedents in support of their
respective contentions. It is well settled that there is no straitjacket formula
for determining the rate of interest and that the same must be fixed having
regard to the facts and circumstances of each case.
9. In the present case, the fire accident occurred on 02.01.2001, the
3

--- Page 280 ---
consumer complaint was filed on 28.02.2003, and the NCDRC passed the
impugned order on 18.08.2025. The dispute has, thus, remained in litigation
for a considerable period. Having regard to the prolonged deprivation of the
appellant of the amount found payable under the insurance claim and the
overall circumstances of the case, we are of the view that the ends of justice
would be served by enhancing the rate of interest from 6% to 9% per
annum on the amount awarded by the NCDRC.  The rate of interest is
accordingly enhanced. Except to the extent of the said modification, the
award of the NCDRC is affirmed in all other respects. 
10. In fine,  the  Civil  Appeal  is disposed  of with  a direction to  the
respondent-insurance company to pay the amount awarded by the NCDRC,
together with interest at the enhanced rate of 9% per annum from the date
of filing of the consumer complaint till the date of realisation, within a
period of eight weeks from today.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
         ………………………………J.
        (R. MAHADEVAN)
        ………………………………J.
        (ALOK ARADHE)

OCTOBER 12, 2026

Order on IA No.273983/2026:
6. This  application  has  been  filed  for  suspension  of
sentence  passed  in  S.T.  Case  No.54/122  of  1998  and
confirmed in Criminal Appeal No.168/1999, whereunder the
applicant – appellant has been convicted for the offences
punishable under Sections 302/34 of the Indian Penal Code,
1860 and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for
2

--- Page 294 ---
life.
7. The case of the prosecution is that on 06.01.1997 at
about 06:00 P .M. at Chandabali Bazar, District – Bhadrak,
Orissa, when the electricity failed, four persons armed with
swords and pistol attacked deceased – Prafulla Nayak near
the tea-cum-sweet stall of Bhikari Sahu and apprehending
danger, the deceased ran into the cabin of a shoe shop
across the road and the attackers chased him and entered
the cabin and inflicted repeated swords blows upon him. It
is  the  further  case  of  the  prosecution  that  when  PW-4
(cousin of the deceased) protested, one of the assailants
showed a revolver and, thereafter, they left the scene of
crime after assaulting the deceased. Police were said to
have taken the injured to the hospital and he was declared
brought dead.
8. According to the prosecution’s story, the assailants,
as stated by PW-6 and PW-7, were the appellant, Laxman @
Dushasan Naik and two others.
9. The  appellant  having  been  incarcerated  for  more
than twelve years on being imposed the sentence of life
3

--- Page 295 ---
imprisonment is seeking for suspension of the same and
has prayed for grant of bail.
10. The credibility of the deposition of PW-6 and PW-7
ought to be evaluated in the teeth of the contentions raised
in the present appeal with regard to there being several
contradictions  including  the  contention  of  PW-4  having
failed to identify the accused, namely, the appellant herein
in  the  T est  Identification  Parade  as  well  as  in  the  dock
during the trial. The prosecution having relied upon the
evidence tendered by PW-4, PW-6 and PW-7 will have to be
examined  or  considered  in  the  background  of  the  post
mortem  report of the deceased, the injuries sustained as
well  as  the  evidence  of  the  doctor,  i.e.,  PW-9,  who
conducted the post mortem.
11. At  this  stage,  the  appreciation  of  the  evidence
undertaken may prejudice either of the parties. Hence, we
desist from undertaking such an exercise. Suffice it to state
that, prima facie,  the contradictions act as a mirror to the
contentions raised by the learned counsel appearing for the
appellant. In this  background, we  are  of  the  considered
4

--- Page 296 ---
view that sentence imposed on the appellant deserves to
be suspended. Accordingly, it is suspended and appellant is
ordered  to  be  released  on  bail  on  such  terms  and
conditions as the jurisdictional Sessions Court may deem fit
to impose. Accordingly, the application stands allowed.
12. The Registry to secure the lower-courts’ records and
on receipt of the same, the soft copies shall be furnished to
the respective learned counsels.

        IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
 CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
 
CIVIL APPEAL NO.     OF 2026 
(@SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION NO.       OF 2026) 
(@SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) Diary No. 25075/2024) 
 
 
BHOLENDRA PRATAP SINGH & ANR.                      Appellants(s) 
 
                                VERSUS 
 
COMMITTEE OF MANAGEMENT & ORS.                     Respondent(s) 
 
 
 
                             O R D E R 
 
1. IA No. 127684/2024 is allowed. 
2. Leave granted. 
3. The appellants/alleged contemnors challenged the order of the 
High Court dated 27.05.2024 which framed charges of contempt 
and fixed the case for 30.05.2024. Since the certified copy was 
not received, appellants approached this Court with expedition 
and later produced the order dated 27.05.2024 by way of an 
application. 
4. The 1st respondent is the Committee of Management of a School, 
which was concerned with the approval for the purpose of 
issuance of advertisement to fill the post of Assistant 
Teachers and that of Headmaster, which were lying vacant. A 
writ petition was filed numbered as Service Single No.17187 of 
2019, which was disposed of directing a decision to be taken in 
terms of the Uttar Pradesh Recognized Basic Schools (Junior 
High Schools) (Recruitment and Conditions of Services of 

--- Page 303 ---
2 
 
Teachers), Rules 1978 1 within a period of two weeks from the 
date of communication of the order. On the allegation that the 
appellants purposefully delayed the consideration and took a 
decision in accordance with the amendments brought to the Rules 
of 1978, a contempt case was filed in which Annexure P3 order 
was passed directing compliance of the judgment; that is 
consideration of the case in accordance with the unamended 
Rules. That having not been done, the Court had passed a 
detailed order on 27.05.2024 in Contempt Application (Civil) 
No.1785 of 2019, summoning the appellants herein. 
5. Admittedly, there was delay in consideration, but however, in 
the meanwhile, there were amendments brought to the Rule. The 
consideration was made in accordance with the amendments 
brought in and despite a requisition being asked for in terms 
of the amended Rules, the 1 st respondent failed to respond. At 
worst, the appellants could be hauled up on contempt for not 
having complied with the directions within the time specified. 
However, the fact remains that the Rules were amended and in a 
contempt petition there could not have been a direction issued 
to consider the issue based on the unamended Rules. The 
reasoning of the High Court seems to be that the Rules were 
amended in the month of December while the time granted by the 
Court, i.e. two weeks, would have ended in July itself. The 1 st 
respondent could definitely challenge  the order in a writ 
petition. However, we are not convinced that there is any case 
made out for contempt. The order in Contempt Application (Civil) 
No.1785 of 2019 dated 27.05.2024 shall stand set aside. The 
 
1 For brevity, ‘the Rules of 1978’ 

--- Page 304 ---
3 
 
contempt applications shall be closed. 
6. The Appeal is allowed. 
7. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand rejected.

(arising out of SLP(Crl.) No. 2927/2026)

1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant, Elizabeth John, assails the judgment and order
dated 04.08.2025 passed by a learned Judge of the High Court of
Kerala, dismissing her Criminal Revision Petition No. 793/2022.
The said revision was filed by her challenging the dismissal of
her discharge petition by the Special Court at Thrissur. 
3. By  order  dated  09.02.2026,  this  Court  directed  further
proceedings in C.C. No. 6/2014 pending before the learned
Enquiry Commissioner and Special Judge, Thrissur, to remain
stayed insofar as they pertained to the appellant.  
4. The appellant was arraigned as Accused No. 13 in C.C. No.
6/2014 arising out of First Information Report (FIR) No. 3/2005
dated  27.01.2005  registered  by  the  Vigilance  and  Anti-
Corruption Bureau, Thrissur, under Section 13(1)(d) read with
Section 13(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988, and
Crl.A. @ SLP(Crl.) No. 2927/2026 1

--- Page 333 ---
Sections 419, 420, 465, 468, 471 and 120B of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860. Pertinent to note, the appellant was not shown as
an accused in the aforestated FIR but she was implicated in the
Final Report dated 31.12.2013.  The offences alleged arose out
of the sanction of two term loans by the Kerala Financial
Corporation1, Thrissur, in the year 2001. Pertinent to note, the
appellant joined the service of the KFC in 1978 and retired in
2006. She was a Deputy Manager (Legal) in 2001 and in that
capacity, she was a member of the District Level Screening
Committee2 of the KFC which processed loan proposals. The
offences alleged relate to two term loans of 50,00,000/-₹
(Rupees fifty lakhs only) each sanctioned by the DLSC in favour
of M/s. Geetha Suppliers and M/s. G & J Suppliers. 
5. The meeting of the DLSC was stated to have been held on
31.03.2001 and the appellant participated as a Deputy Manager
(Legal). The Regional Manager of KFC, viz., K.S.V. Nayakan, was
the Chairman of the DLSC and he was shown as Accused No. 10.
Significantly, his discharge application in Criminal M.P. No.
323/2015 in C.C. No. 6/2014 was allowed by the learned Enquiry
Commissioner & Special Judge, Thrissur.  This order attained
finality  as  the  State  did  not  choose  to  challenge  it.
Similarly, Bhaskaran K.P., Accused No. 14, was also discharged
by the learned Enquiry Commissioner & Special Judge, Thrissur,
vide  order  dated  07.10.2021  passed  in  Criminal  M.P.  No.
788/2016 in C.C. No. 6/2014.  The same relief was extended to
1  “KFC”, for short
2  “DLSC”, for short
Crl.A. @ SLP(Crl.) No. 2927/2026 2

--- Page 334 ---
M.V. Antony, Accused No. 16, by way of order dated 09.05.2022
passed in Criminal M.P. No. 789/2016 in C.C. No. 6/2014.  
6. However, the discharge application filed by the appellant in
Criminal M.P. No. 787/2016 in C.C. No. 6/2014 was dismissed by
the learned Enquiry Commissioner & Special Judge, Thrissur,
vide order dated 29.08.2022, on the ground that she failed to
scrutinize the documents and misused her official position as a
Deputy Manager (Legal).  Aggrieved thereby, the appellant filed
Criminal Revision Petition No. 793/2022, which came to be
dismissed by the High Court,  vide  judgment and order dated
04.08.2025, which is impugned presently.
7. The State of Kerala filed a counter affidavit before this
Court.  Therein,  the  State  did  not  attempt  to  draw  any
distinction between the cases of the other accused who stood
discharged and the case of the appellant.  It may be noted that
the appellant was only a Deputy Manager (Legal) and was a
member of the DLSC in that capacity. The Chairman of the DLSC,
viz., K.S.V. Nayakan, Accused No. 10, would obviously have a
bigger role and responsibility in vetting loan proposals and
sanctioning loans. Unless specific allegations are levelled
against the appellant in the context of her deliberately
failing to carry out her duties as a Deputy Manager (Legal) in
scrutinizing the loan proposals, the question of proceeding
against her, while letting off other members of the DLSC, who
clearly  had  a  bigger  role  and  responsibility,  cannot  be
countenanced.  We find no such attempt having been made by the
Crl.A. @ SLP(Crl.) No. 2927/2026 3

--- Page 335 ---
State. On the other hand, the State admitted candidly that
there was no prima facie case against those accused who already
stood discharged. In the light of this admission in the context
of the Chairman of the DLSC who obviously had a much bigger
role and responsibility in sanctioning loans, we find no reason
to allow the case to proceed against the appellant who, by her
very designation, had a much smaller role to play.
8. The appeal is, accordingly, allowed, setting aside the impugned
judgment and order dated 04.8.2025.  
9. The appellant, Elizabeth John, shall stand discharged in C.C.
No. 6/2014 on the file of the learned Enquiry Commissioner &
Special Judge, Thrissur, under Section 239 of the Code of
Criminal Procedure, 1973.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

    O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The  Labour  Court  passed  an  Award  in  favour  of  the
appellant(s) on 13.08.2009 directing payment of compensation
of Rs.1,00,000/-in lieu of reinstatement after holding that
his termination was in violation of provision under Section
25-F of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The cheque for this
amount was handed over to the appellant on 21.09.2010. 
3. Appellant preferred Writ Petition before the High Court
which was dismissed on 09.08.2018. The appellant thereafter
approached the Division Bench of the High Court by preferring
an intra-court appeal, LPA No. 1782 of 2018 (O&M). The said
LPA  was  decided  on  12.09.2024  allowing  compensation  of
Rs.6,00,000/- in favour of the appellant to be paid within 30
days failing which it shall carry interest at the rate of 8
per cent p.a. from the date of passing of the Award i.e,
13.08.2009.

--- Page 338 ---
2
4. Thereafter, the respondent preferred Review Petition RA-
LP No. 26/25 in which, the learned Division Bench of the High
Court modified the earlier order to direct payment of interest
from 12.09.2024 instead of 13.08.2009.
5. Admittedly, the respondent has failed to deposit the
amount of compensation of Rs.6,00,000/- within the stipulated
time of 30 days from 12.09.2024 i.e. from the date the first
order was passed by the Division Bench of the High Court.
6. In our considered view, the Division Bench of the High
Court ought not to have modified the earlier order considering
that there was no mistake or error apparent on the face of the
record and the same was reviewed by taking a lenient view on
the respondent.
7. Since, the amount of compensation as initially awarded by
the Labour Court has been enhanced by the High Court as a
necessary corollary upon default in payment of the enhanced
compensation, it would carry interest from the date of Award
and there is no justification for the High Court to have
subsequently modified the order making payment of the interest
component from 12.09.2024 and not from the date of the Award.
8. In view of the above, we set aside the impugned order
passed in Review Petition bearing RA-LP No.26/25 by the High
Court and restore the earlier order passed by the High Court
in LPA No. 1782 of 2018 (O&M) on 12.09.2024.  Since the
earlier order of the High Court has been restored, the same
shall be complied with within three months from today.

--- Page 339 ---
3

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.           OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO.9639/2026)
GURWINDER SINGH      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
STATE OF PUNJAB     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned counsel for the respondent-State of Punjab.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 02.08.2025
passed  by  the  High  Court  of  Punjab  and  Haryana  at
Chandigarh  (briefly  the  ‘High  Court’  hereinafter),
rejecting the regular bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant is an accused in FIR No.115/2023 registered
at Police Station- Sadar, Bathinda, District- Bathinda,
Punjab under Sections 302, 323, 148 and 149 of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’) (Section 325 of IPC
was added later on).
5. According to the prosecution, on 18.07.2023 at about
05:00 PM, the complainant received telephonic information
that his son Jashandeep Singh was injured in a fight and
1

--- Page 358 ---
had been taken to the Civil Hospital at Bathinda. When he
met his son in the Civil Hospital, the son told him that
Ranjit Singh, Gurwinder Singh @ Guri (appellant herein)
and Amanjeet Singh @ Amana, along with 10-12 other unknown
persons had assaulted him with baseball bats and daang.
His son was thereafter shifted to Badiyal Hospital at
Bathinda, where he succumbed to his injuries.
6. This  Court  had  issued  notice  vide  order  dated
13.05.2026.
7. In  the  proceedings  held  on  24.07.2026,  learned
Advocate General, who had appeared for the respondent-
State of Punjab, made a statement that the informant
Jagsir Singh was examined. However, his cross-examination
was yet to take place. Thereafter, on a couple of dates,
the  matter  was  deferred  as  the  cross-examination  of
informant Jagsir Singh could not be carried out for one
reason or the other. Now the cross-examination has been
fixed on 11.11.2026.
8. Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  submits  that
appellant  was  arrested  on  23.07.2023.  Though  he  was
granted interim bail by the High Court, subsequently the
bail order was withdrawn. His further submission is that
till date 04 accused have been granted bail by the Trial
Court and by the High Court. Only the appellant continues
to remain behind bars. He also submits that appellant is
not the main accused.
9. On  the  other  hand,  learned  counsel  for  the
2

--- Page 359 ---
respondent-State of Punjab submits that though on the
previous  occasion,  a  statement  was  made  that  cross-
examination  of  Jagsir  Singh  would  be  recorded  on
12.10.2026, the same could not be done as the Presiding
Officer of the Trial Court was transferred. Now, a new
Presiding Officer has joined the Court; he has fixed
11.11.2026 as the date for cross-examination of Jagsir
Singh. He also submits that after the High Court had
earlier withdrawn the bail order, appellant had evaded and
did not surrender. This factor also may be taken into
consideration.
10. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and on
due consideration, while we are conscious of the fact that
appellant had jumped bail on an earlier occasion, we are,
however, of the opinion that having regard to the fact
that there has been a delay in the trial and that several
co-accused have been granted bail, similar benefit may
also be extended to the appellant.
11. That being the position, t he impugned order dated
02.08.2025 passed by the High Court is set aside.
12. Consequently, we direct that the appellant shall be
produced before the Trial Court within a maximum period of
07 days from today, whereafter he shall be released on
bail on such terms and conditions as may be deemed
appropriate. Additionally, we make it clear that appellant
shall appear before the Trial Court on the dates fixed by
the Court, except on such occasions where his personal
3

--- Page 360 ---
presence may be exempted by the Court.
13. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
14. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.
…………………………………………………...J.

…………………………………………………...J.

2. The present Special Leave Petition calls in question the

Case No.3147 of 2025 in Criminal Writ Jurisdiction Case No.1696
of 2025.  By the said order, the High Court directed the
concerned Circle Officer to issue notice to the khatal owner
(petitioner herein) for removal of encroachment, and if the
khatal owner does not remove, then the Circle Officer concerned
and the SHO of Kankarbag Police Station to take appropriate
steps for removal of the encroachment on the land in question.
3. The grievance of the petitioner, who has challenged the
order, is that when the impugned order was passed, he was not
heard.  Learned counsel has a further grievance that even in
the main Criminal Writ Jurisdiction Case No.1696 of 2025, which
was filed by respondent Nos.7 and 8 herein, the petitioner was
not arrayed as a party. 
4. The petitioner has, on 12th December 2025, filed an IA No.
1 of 2025, in Criminal Writ Jurisdiction Case No. 1696 of 2025
for impleadment. Pending that petition, respondent Nos. 7 and 8
filed a Miscellaneous Jurisdiction Case No. 3147 of 2025 for
implementing and carrying out an order of 24th July 2025 made in
the  pending  Writ  Petition.  The  said  order  recorded  the
undertaking of the SHO Kankarbagh, Patna, to the effect that he
will take necessary action in the light of certain earlier
orders passed by the Court in CWJC No. 2290 of 1990 (Arun Kumar
2

--- Page 369 ---
Mukherjee & Ors.  v  The State of Bihar & Ors.) .   The net
result is that the petitioner was neither impleaded in the Writ
Petition nor in the Miscellaneous Jurisdiction Case No. 3147 of
2025. 
5. Being aggrieved, the petitioner approached this Court by
filing the present petition.  When the matter came up before
this Court on 21st April 2026, while granting permission to file
the Special Leave Petition and issuing notice, this Court
granted status quo. 
6. While the stand of the petitioner is that notwithstanding
the status quo, demolitions were carried out, the stand of the
State, as well as the Writ Petitioners (who are respondent Nos.
7 and 8 herein) in the High Court, is that the demolitions were
carried out prior to the order of status quo. Learned counsel
appearing for respondent Nos. 7 and 8 (Writ Petitioners)
submits that post the demolition, there is a reconstruction of
the  structure.  That  is  a  matter  for  the  High  Court  to
adjudicate in the pending Writ Petition. The parties may place
these facts also before the High Court.     
7. We dispose of the present Special Leave Petition by
directing that the petitioner will be impleaded both in the
Writ Petition and in the Contempt Case, and the Writ Petition
and the Contempt Case will be disposed of after giving him an
opportunity of hearing.
8. We also reserve liberty to the petitioner to work out his
rights.
3

--- Page 370 ---
9. All contentions between the parties are left open. 
10. The special leave petition is disposed of in the above
terms.
11. Pending application, if any, shall stand disposed of.

DEV KUMAR PASWAN                              Petitioner

IA No. 253611/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING C/C OF THE

IA No. 253612/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.
IA No. 254798/2026 - PERMISSION TO FILE ADDITIONAL 
DOCUMENTS/FACTS/ ANNEXURES
 
Date : 14-10-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE DIPANKAR DATTA
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE SHEEL NAGU
For Petitioner(s) :Ms. Fauzia Shakil, Adv.
                   Ms. Tanya Srivastava, AOR
                   Ms. Kushank Mittal, Adv.
                   Mr. Anmol Kheta, Adv.
                   Mr. Dinesh Kumar, Adv.
                                      
For Respondent(s) :Mr. Akshay Amritanshu- 3121, AOR
                   Mr. Sarthak Srivastava, Adv.
                   Mr. Utkarsh Rai, Adv.
     UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                         O R D E R
1. Ms. Fauzia Shakil, learned counsel appearing for the petitioner,
has drawn our attention to an order dated 13 th May, 2026 passed by
the High Court of Judicature at Patna granting bail to a co-accused,

--- Page 416 ---
2
i.e., Sanjay Singh Bhokta @ Sanjay Singh.
2. It appears that the said accused, incarcerated since 24 th July,
2025  and  also  having  an  antecedent,  was  granted  bail  on  the
following terms:
“8. It  is  made  clear  that  the  learned  trial  Court
before  releasing  the  petitioner  on  bail  shall  verify
whether charges against the petitioner has been framed
or not if it is found that charges against the petitioner has
not been framed in that event the present order shall not
be given effect to, but if it is found that charges against
the  petitioner  stands  framed  then  petitioner  will  be
released forthwith.”
3. Petitioner  and  co-accused,  Sanjay  Singh  Bhokta,  along  with
others  figure  as  accused  in  First  Information  Report1 dated  8 th
November, 2018 under Sections 147, 148, 149, 307, 353, 504, 506,
120-B of the Indian Penal Code, 1860; Sections 25(1-B), 26, 27 and 35
of  the  Arms  Act,  1959;  Sections  3,  4  and  5  of  the  Explosive
Substances Act, 1908; and Sections 16, 18 and 20 of the Unlawful
Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967 (UAPA), registered by Police Station
Dumariya, District Gaya, Bihar.
4. Ms. Shakil submits that while the petitioner was not named in
the  FIR,  the  said  accused  Sanjay  Singh  Bhokta  is  an  FIR  named
accused who came to be arrested two months’ after the petitioner
had surrendered. She also submits that the petitioner stands on a
better footing and is, thus, entitled to claim parity.
5. Ms.  Shakil  also  draws  our  attention  to  paragraph  29  of  the
1 FIR

--- Page 417 ---
3
counter affidavit filed by the respondent - State of Bihar where it is
averred as follows:
“29. It is submitted that charge could not be framed
as the Petitioner, a non-FIR named accused, has not been
produced from jail before the Ld. Trial Court.”
6. For  want  of  adequate  instructions,  Mr.  Akshay  Amritanshu,
learned counsel appearing for the State of Bihar is unable to throw
light as to why for a period of almost 14 months, i.e., 10 th May, 2025
(date on which the petitioner surrendered) till 29 th July, 2025 (date on
which supplementary charge sheet was filed), the petitioner could not
be produced before  the  trial court and why charge  has not been
framed till date. Indeed, if what is disclosed in the affidavit is correct,
it is surprising that the trial court has also not required the petitioner
to be produced before it!
7. Be that as it may, we are  prima facie  of the view that the
petitioner stands on a better footing than Sanjay Singh Bhokta and,
therefore, we direct his release on interim bail, to be operative till the
next date  of hearing, subject to such terms  and conditions to be
imposed by the trial court.
8. The investigating officer of the case shall submit a report before
this  Court  indicating  the  real  reason  for  non-production  of  the
petitioner before the trial court, which as per the aforesaid affidavit,
has contributed to non-framing of charges against him.
9. At the same time, we require the Registrar General of the High

--- Page 418 ---
4
Court to obtain a report from the relevant trial court with regard to the
undesirable development that has been noted above. Such report
must be placed before the Registry of this Court in a sealed cover by
15th November, 2026.
10. Re-list the special leave petition on 17th November, 2026.
(JATINDER KAUR)                       (SUDHIR KUMAR SHARMA)

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL Nos.                      OF 2026
[arising out of SLP (Crl.) Nos. 17270-17271 OF 2026]
 
GANESH HARIBHAU GAIKWAD                     APPELLANT
                            VERSUS
THE STATE OF MAHARASHTRA                    RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The  High  Court  of  Judicature  at  Bombay,  Circuit  Bench  at
Kolhapur, by the impugned judgment and order dated 13th February,
2026, has dismissed the appellant’s applications1 for regular bail.
3. Appellant was arrested on 21 st October, 2024 in connection
with two FIRs, viz. (1) FIR No. 0940 of 2024 dated 21st October, 2024
and (2) FIR No. 1059 of 2024 dated 20 th November, 2024, both
under Sections 170, 420, 465, 467, 468, 469, 470, 471, 472 and
473 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860; Section 66(C) of the Information
T echnology  Act,  2000  registered  at  Police  Station-Satara  City,
District-Satara, Maharashtra.
1 Bail Application Nos. 3427 and 3647 of 2025

--- Page 420 ---
2
4. We have heard learned counsel appearing for the parties and
perused the materials on record.
5. Police reports (charge-sheets) have been filed on 18 th January,
2025 in FIR No. 0940 of 2024 and on 17 th January, 2025 in FIR No.
1059 of 2024; however, the charges have yet not been framed. As
and when trial commences, it will take some time to conclude. That
apart, the case is triable by a magistrate.
6. Additionally, it is evident from the counter affidavit filed by
the  respondent  –  State  of  Maharashtra  that  all  incriminating
materials, which the prosecution proposes to rely on to establish the
charges against the appellant, have been collected. Thus, there is
little reason to keep him under detention any longer.
7. T aking an overall view of the matter, we are of the considered
opinion that the appellant could be admitted to an order for release
on bail pending trial.
8. Accordingly, we set aside the impugned judgment and order.
9. Appellant shall be released on bail, subject to furnishing of
bail bonds to the satisfaction of the trial court and subject to such
other terms and conditions as may be imposed by it.
10. Needless  to  observe,  the  appellant  shall  not,  directly  or
indirectly, by making inducement, threat or promise, dissuade any
person acquainted with the facts of the case from disclosing such
facts to the court.

--- Page 421 ---
3
11. In the event there is any breach of the terms and conditions
for grant of bail, the trial court shall be at liberty to cancel the bail
of the appellant.
12. It is  also ordered that the appellant shall diligently attend
proceedings  of  the  trial,  unless  exempted.  If  he  abstains  from
attending the proceedings without justifiable cause, that could also
be seen as breach of the conditions for grant of bail and the trial
court will be free to pass appropriate orders.
13. We clarify that the observations made in this order and grant
of bail will not be treated as findings on the merits of the case.
14. The appeals are, accordingly, allowed on the aforesaid terms.
15. Pending interlocutory application(s), if any, stand disposed of.

[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated 29-05-

GOVIND SINGH RAJPUT                                Petitioner(s)
                                VERSUS
STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH & ANR.                     Respondent(s)
IA No. 194144/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING C/C OF THE IMPUGNED
JUDGMENT, IA No. 194143/2026 - EXEMPTION FROM FILING O.T.
 
Date : 13-10-2026 This matter was called on for hearing today.
CORAM :  HON'BLE THE CHIEF JUSTICE
         HON'BLE MR. JUSTICE JOYMALYA BAGCHI
         HON'BLE MRS. JUSTICE V. MOHANA
For Petitioner(s) :Mr. Vivek Ranjan Pandey, Adv.
                   Ms. Shambhavi Shrivastava, Adv.
                   Mr. Padmesh Mishra, Adv.
                   M/s. Brajesh Pandey & Associates- 3865, AOR
                                      
For Respondent(s) :Ms. Mrinal Gopal Elker- 2566, AOR
                   Ms. Sai Shashank, Adv.
                   Ms. Silpi S Swain, Adv.
                   
                   Mr. Yashaswi S.k. Chocksey- 4329, AOR
                   
          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Pursuant to our order dated 21.09.2026, the State of Madhya
Pradesh has filed a compliance affidavit stating,  inter alia,
that the Assistant Superintendent of Police, Bina, directed the
SHO, Police Station Malthone, on 23.09.2026 and 26.09.2026, to
1

--- Page 448 ---
ensure strict compliance with our order. The Collector, District
Sagar, thereafter fixed the demarcation under Section 129 of the
Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Code, 1959, for 29.09.2026, with
notice to the parties. Respondent No. 2-complainant was called
to the spot, and notice was also issued to various persons,
including the adjoining landholders. The demarcation was carried
out by Rover machine in the presence of the Collector, the
Superintendent of Police, Respondent No. 2 and the adjoining
landholders, and the exercise was videographed. The half share
of Respondent No. 2 in the subject land, i.e., Khasra No. 70,
admeasuring 1.23 hectares, situated in Village Chakk Baghhoniya,
Tehsil  Malthone,  District  Sagar,  being  0.615  hectare,  was
demarcated. Stone pillars were erected, the land was ploughed
and physical possession was handed over to Respondent No. 2.
2. The SHO, Police Station Malthone, has filed a separate
Report stating that possession was handed over without any
hindrance, and that surveillance and patrolling in the area are
continuing.
3. Learned State counsel submits that the directions issued by
this Court stand complied with. Learned counsel for Respondent
No. 2-complainant also acknowledges that peaceful possession at
the spot has been handed over to Respondent No. 2 in the manner
set out in the compliance affidavit. She, however, expresses an
apprehension  that,  given  the  criminal  antecedents  of  the
petitioner and his alleged involvement in several cases of land
grabbing, the possession of Respondent No. 2 over the subject
2

--- Page 449 ---
land may be disturbed.
4. We have considered the submissions proferred by the learned
Counsel before us, and perused the relevant record.
 5. To ensure that Respondent No. 2 continues to enjoy peaceful
possession of her share in the subject land, we dispose of this
petition in the following terms:
(i) The interim protection granted to the petitioner vide order
dated 17.07.2026 is made absolute, subject to the condition that
neither the petitioner nor his associates, nor any person acting
at his behest, shall make any attempt, directly or indirectly,
to dispossess Respondent No. 2 from the subject land, extend any
threat  to  her,  or  otherwise  interfere  with  her  possession
thereof;
(ii) Upon receipt of any complaint from Respondent No. 2 alleging
a breach of the condition in clause (i), the SHO, Police Station
Malthone,  shall  register  an  FIR  without  conducting  any
preliminary inquiry. The State of Madhya Pradesh shall forthwith
report  the  matter  to  this  Court,  whereupon  the  protection
granted to the petitioner shall be liable to be withdrawn;
(iii) We make it clear that if the petitioner is found to be

1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard Ms. Bharti Tyagi, learned counsel
for the appellant and Ms. Sakshi Kakkar, learned
1

--- Page 452 ---
counsel for the respondent-State of Uttar Pradesh.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 05.02.2026
passed by the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad
(briefly,  ‘the  High  Court’  hereinafter),  partly
allowing the Criminal Appeal of the appellant.
4. It is stated that appellant along with another,
were convicted by the Court of Additional Sessions
Judge (Fast Track Court)-I, Bareilly in Sessions
Trial No.388/2014 under Sections 307/34, 504 and 506
of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short, ‘IPC’),
vide the judgment and order dated 21.03.2025 and
sentenced to undergo imprisonment for life for the
offence under Section 307/34 of IPC and to pay a fine
of Rs.50,000/- each with a default stipulation and
other lesser sentences.
5. Aggrieved  by  the  conviction  and  sentence  as
aforesaid, appellant and another preferred Criminal
Appeal No.3265 of 2025 before the High Court.
6. Vide  the  impugned  judgment  and  order  dated
05.02.2026, the High Court modified the conviction
imposed by the Trial Court by holding that the
appellant and the other convict stood convicted only
under Sections 323 and 324/34 of IPC. The conviction
under  Section  307/34  of  IPC  was  found  to  be
unsustainable  and  accordingly,  the  appellant  was
acquitted of the charge under Section 307/34 of IPC.
Consequently, the sentence imposed on the appellant
2

--- Page 453 ---
and the other convict was also modified from life
imprisonment to 03 years with fine of Rs.5,000/-
under Section 324/34 of IPC; while the sentence
awarded under Section 506 of IPC was reduced from 07
years imprisonment to one of 03 years with fine of
Rs.10,000/-; both the sentences were directed to run
concurrently.
7. In other words, the sentence of the appellant was
reduced from life imprisonment to 03 years.
8. On 18.08.2026, we had issued notice, both on the
Special Leave Petition as well as on the prayer for
bail.
9. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that
out of the sentence of 03 years, appellant has
undergone incarceration for about 18 months, which is
more than 50%.
10. To this, learned counsel for the respondent-State
of Uttar Pradesh submits that already the High Court
has taken a very lenient view and has reduced the
sentence  significantly.  Therefore,  suspending  the
modified sentence and enlarging the appellant on
bail, may not be warranted.
11. After hearing learned counsel for the parties and
on due consideration, we are satisfied that the
modified sentence imposed on the appellant may be
suspended and the appellant may be enlarged on bail
during the pendency of the appeal before this Court.
3

--- Page 454 ---
12. Consequently, we direct that the sentence imposed
on the appellant, as modified, shall remain suspended
during pendency of the appeal before this Court and
the appellant shall be released on bail on usual
terms and conditions.
13. List the Criminal Appeal for hearing in due
course.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.           OF 2026
(@ SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (CRIMINAL) NO.14319/2026)
ANIL KUMAR      APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE SENIOR INTELLIGENCE OFFICER     RESPONDENT(S)
ORDER
1. Leave granted.
2. We have heard Mr. Priyanshu Upadhyay, learned counsel
for the appellant and  Mr. Anil Kaushik,  learned Addl.
Solicitor General for the respondent.
3. Appellant is aggrieved by order dated 28.03.2025
passed by the High Court of Andhra Pradesh at Amaravati
(briefly the ‘High Court’ hereinafter), rejecting the
regular bail application of the appellant.
4. Appellant is an accused in N.S.C. No.04/2023 arising
out of F.No.-DRI/HZU/VRU/48/ENQ-02 (INT-02/2022).
5. As per the prosecution, officials of the Directorate
of  Revenue  Intelligence  (for  short,  ‘DRI’)  recovered
1169.30  kgs  of  ganja  from  a  TATA  truck  which  was
intercepted at Gobburu at Kasimkota in the district of
Anakapalle,  Andhra  Pradesh  on  17.04.2022.  It  further
1

--- Page 456 ---
appears that the investigating agency issued summons to
the appellant whereafter he was arrested on 21.07.2022
based  on  his  confessional  statement  made  before  the
officials of the DRI. Since then, he has been in custody.
6. This  Court  had  issued  notice  vide  order  dated
03.08.2026, pursuant to which respondent has filed counter
affidavit.
7. Learned counsel for the appellant submits that no
recovery of any contraband was made from the person of the
appellant. No one, other than the appellant, has been
arrested. He has no criminal antecedent. Investigation is
complete,  whereafter  charge-sheet  was  filed.  Though
charges have been framed, the trial has not commenced.
8. Learned counsel for the appellant has also produced
before us the Record of Proceedings before the Trial Court
which shows that the appellant was not produced before the
Trial Court from the Central Prison, Visakhapatnam where
he has been put in custody.
9. Per contra , Mr. Kaushik, learned Addl. Solicitor
General  appearing  for  the  respondent  submits  that
appellant was the driver of the truck from where the
seizure was made. However, he fairly admits that trial has
not commenced and appellant has also not been produced
before the Trial Court by the jail authorities.
10. While we express our surprise and concern at the
conduct of the jail authorities in not producing the
appellant before the Trial Court on the dates fixed, thus
2

--- Page 457 ---
frustrating the cause of justice, we are also aware of the
fact that appellant has been in custody for more than 04
years now. Having regard to the fact that there is no
criminal antecedent of the appellant and no recovery was
made from him, we are inclined to grant bail to the
appellant.
11. That being the position, t he impugned order dated
28.03.2025 passed by the High Court is set aside.
12. Consequently, we direct that the appellant shall be
produced before the Trial Court within a maximum period of
07 days from today, whereafter he shall be released on
bail on such terms and conditions as may be deemed
appropriate.
13. Needless to say, both the parties shall co-operate
with the trial.
14. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal is allowed.
15. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

1. We have heard learned counsel for the parties.
2. Having been denied promotion to the post of
Junior Operator (Control Room) from the post of
Fireman, the petitioner had filed a Writ Petition 1
before the High Court2.
1  WP(C) No.222 of 2023
2  High Court of Tripura, Agartala
1

--- Page 498 ---
3. The said Writ Petition was opposed by the State-
respondent on the ground that the Department had
asked  for  options  from  the  employees  and  the
deadline  for  submitting  those  options  was
18.09.2021. Within the said deadline, no option was
exercised and, therefore, the writ petitioner was
not entitled to promotion.
4. The High Court vide order dated 07.07.2023 found
that the respondent had not adhered to the time
limits and had considered promotion of an employee
who had given an option on 20.09.2021. Besides, the
High Court was of the view that sufficient time was
not provided to the employees to exercise their
option. Accordingly, the High Court directed the
respondents to treat the petitioner as having opted
for  promotion  and  consider  the  request  of  the
petitioner for promotion to the post of Junior
Operator (Control Room) in accordance with law,
subject to existence of a vacancy on the post of
Junior Operator (Control Room).
5. Based on the aforesaid direction given by the
High Court, the State-respondent  vide order dated
03.10.2023  rejected  the  representation  of  the
petitioner for promotion  inter alia  on the ground
that there exists no vacancy on the post of Junior
Operator (Control Room).
6. Aggrieved  by  the  rejection  of  his
2

--- Page 499 ---
representation,  the  petitioner  filed  a  fresh
petition which stood dismissed by the Single Judge
Bench and thereafter the Division Bench dismissed
the writ appeal by the impugned order.
7. As we find that there is no challenge to the
finding returned in the order dated 03.10.2023 that
there is no vacancy to the post of Junior Operator
(Control Room), having regard to the fact that the
earlier direction of the High Court was to operate
in case there existed a vacancy on the post of
Junior Operator (Control Room), we do not find a
good reason to interfere with the impugned order,
the  special  leave  petition  is,  accordingly,
dismissed.
8. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  stand
disposed of.

Corporation  under  the  provisions  of  Section  264(1)  of  the
Maharashtra Municipal Corporation Act, 1949 (for short, the “Act of
1949”) and a further challenge to the constitutional validity of
Section 433A of the Act of 1949 since it bars the questioning of a
Notice issued under Section 264 of the Act of 1949 in any suit or
legal proceedings. The appellants before us claim to be tenants of
a building which had to be demolished by the Corporation on the
ground that the same was in a dilapidated condition and would have
led to some casualties if the building would have collapsed . It is
not in dispute that at the relevant point of time, after serving
the Notice under Section 264(1) of the Act of 1949, the building
was brought down.

3. Nothing further survives in the matter.

entitlement to have appropriate accommodation in the new building
that is coming up, it shall be open for them to take up this issue
with the competent authority in accordance with law. 
5. With the aforesaid liberty, this appeal stands disposed of.

SLP(Crl.) Nos. 15490/2026 and 15158/2026
The counter affidavits filed by the State of Andhra Pradesh in
these special leave petitions disclose that the petitioners have
past criminal antecedents.  However, the same have not been
disclosed in the special leave petitions.
In the light of the law laid down by this Court in “Munnesh
vs. State of Uttar Pradesh” 1, the failure to disclose full details
of the past criminal cases registered against them is fatal to the
petitioners’ cases. The special leave petitions are, accordingly,
dismissed on that short ground.
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
SLP(Crl.) Nos. 15307/2026 and 15259/2026
The matters are adjourned to enable the learned counsel for
the State of Andhra Pradesh to get proper instructions as to
whether the petitioners have approached the police to join the
investigation after the interim order dated 31.08.2026 was passed
by this Court.

No. 15259/2026 shall be completed before the next date of hearing.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
CIVIL APPEAL NOs. ______ OF 2026
[SPECIAL LEAVE PETITION (C) Nos. 5096-5097/2026]
CHANCHALBEN MAGANBHAI PATEL                   Appellant (s)
                                VERSUS
MANIBEN MADHUBHAI BOBAA & ORS.                Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. These appeals are against the judgment and order
passed by the High Court of Judicature of Bombay in Appeal
From Order (AFO) Nos. 399 of 2023 and 400 of 2023 dated
10.12.2025.  By  these  orders,  High  Court  reversed  the
temporary injunction order passed by the Trial Court on
13.09.2022, pending disposal of the civil suit. 
3. The short facts, relevant for disposal of these civil
appeals are that, while the appellant/plaintiff filed his
suit for declaration on the basis of relinquishment deed,
the respondent also instituted a parallel suit seeking
declaration that the relinquishment deed is void.
4. As indicated above, while the Trial Court granted an
order  of  injunction  on  the  ground  that  there  is  a
presumption of validity of the relinquishment deed and
that balance of convenience lay with the appellant, the
High Court by the order impugned before us reversed the
order of injunction.

--- Page 549 ---
2
5. While issuing notice in the special leave petition,
this Court, by order dated 13.02.2026 has granted an
interim order directing the parties to maintain status quo
as regards possession.
6. Heard  learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  and  the
respondents. Having considered the matter in detail, we
are of the opinion that interests of both the parties can
be secured if we direct that the order of status quo be
continued till the suit is taken up and disposed of by the
Trial Court. The learned counsel for the appellant and the
respondents  are  also  in  agreement  with  the  said
arrangement. 
7. In view of the above, the civil appeals against the
judgment and order of the High Court of Bombay in Appeal
From  Order  Nos.  399  of  2023  and  400  of  2023  dated
10.12.2025  are  allowed,  and  in  modification  of  the
judgment and order passed by the High Court, we direct
that the parties shall maintain the status quo as regards
suit schedule properties pending disposal of RCS No. 32 of
2017 and SCS No. 22 of 2019.
8. Pending interlocutory application(s), if any, is/are
disposed of.
